lectures.title: Histology of the Small & Large Intestines
Pathology of the Liver & Biliary Tract

questions.q: Which of the following secretions is the most acidic?
questions.ex: Gastric secretion is far more acidic than the other GI secretions, which cluster in the neutral-to-alkaline range.

questions.q: All of the following are secreted by pancreatic acinar cells EXCEPT:
questions.ex: Pepsin(ogen) is a gastric chief-cell product, not pancreatic. HCl converts pepsinogen to pepsin in the stomach.

questions.q: Where is the Na+–bile acid cotransporter located?
questions.ex: Bile salts are reabsorbed via a Na+–bile acid cotransporter in the terminal ileum as part of the enterohepatic circulation.

questions.q: Which substance must be digested further before intestinal absorption?
questions.ex: Only monosaccharides are absorbed. Disaccharides like sucrose (and lactose, maltose) must first be split by brush-border enzymes.

questions.q: Which is characteristic of saliva?
questions.ex: Saliva is hypotonic with high HCO3-, contains alpha-amylase and lingual lipase, and is driven by parasympathetic (not sympathetic) input — abolished by vagotomy. Fuller's lecture draws this comparison directly against pancreatic ductal secretion.

questions.q: A 53-year-old woman has dysphagia, substernal pain worse after large meals and lying down, and melena. Which sphincter is dysfunctional?
questions.ex: This is reflux esophagitis from an incompetent lower esophageal sphincter — classic GERD, worse with large meals and recumbency.

questions.q: A man on a high-protein, low-carb diet needs more pancreatic enzyme secretion to digest it. Which peptide drives this?
questions.ex: CCK is released by peptides, amino acids, and fatty acids in the small intestine and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion.

questions.q: A child with failure to thrive has an enteropeptidase (enterokinase) deficiency. Levels of which enzyme are most affected?
questions.ex: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen → trypsin, which then activates the rest of the protease cascade. Without it, protein digestion collapses.

questions.q: A patient with a gastrin-secreting pancreatic tumor (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) is expected to show:
questions.ex: Excess gastrin drives acid secretion, peptic ulcers, and parietal cell hyperplasia. Lipid absorption actually falls, since the low luminal pH inactivates pancreatic lipase; beta cells are unaffected.

questions.q: Micelle formation is necessary for intestinal absorption of:
questions.ex: Fat-soluble vitamin D needs micelles to stay solubilized in the aqueous lumen until it reaches the enterocyte. Glycerol is water-soluble and doesn't need micelles.

questions.q: Which substance both damages the gastric mucosal barrier and stimulates acid secretion?
questions.ex: H. pylori's urease converts urea to ammonia, which damages the mucosal barrier while also increasing parietal cell mass and acid output.

questions.q: Pepsinogen is secreted mainly from:
questions.ex: Chief (peptic) cells of the gastric gland secrete pepsinogen, converted to active pepsin by HCl or by pepsin itself.

questions.q: A 13-year-old with tremor, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and elevated liver enzymes most likely has accumulation of:
questions.ex: Wilson disease — copper accumulates in the liver, brain (motor symptoms), and eye (Kayser-Fleischer ring at Descemet's membrane).

questions.q: A 60-year-old with 20 years of epigastric pain relieved by food/antacids, on high-dose NSAIDs, now has a bleeding duodenal ulcer. What's the key association?
questions.ex: Duodenal ulcers are strongly linked to H. pylori, which both increases acid secretion and impairs mucosal defenses; NSAIDs compound the injury via COX inhibition.

questions.q: Back-flux of acid plus a weak lower esophageal sphincter causes:
questions.ex: GERD is chronic acid reflux from an incompetent LES. Achalasia is a motility disorder; Mallory-Weiss is a mucosal tear from vomiting; hiatal hernia is structural. Left untreated, GERD progresses to Barrett's esophagus.

questions.q: An autopsy reveals a soft, yellow, greasy, enlarged liver with lipid pushing hepatocyte nuclei to the periphery. Most likely cause?
questions.ex: This is hepatic steatosis. Several things cause it, but alcohol abuse is by far the most common cause in industrialized nations.

questions.q: Ulcers unresponsive to cimetidine, elevated gastrin, jejunal ulcers — suspect Zollinger-Ellison. Best agent?
questions.ex: Omeprazole (a PPI) is preferred once H2-blocker therapy has failed and in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome specifically.

questions.q: Watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, elevated VIP from a pancreatic VIPoma — best agent?
questions.ex: Octreotide (a somatostatin analog) is used for VIPomas, gastrinomas, and glucagonomas to control the secretory diarrhea.

questions.q: Best drug to treat Crohn's disease in a 53-year-old woman?
questions.ex: Sulfasalazine (a 5-ASA) treats inflammatory conditions like Crohn's and ulcerative colitis.

questions.q: A man with a septic hip joint has enteric-smelling drainage and a history of colicky abdominal pain and diarrhea. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.ex: Crohn's disease is notorious for fistula formation — even to unusual sites like a hip joint. Ulcerative colitis rarely fistulizes.

questions.q: Four years after total gastrectomy, a patient develops anemia and neurological signs with megaloblastic marrow changes. Deficient vitamin?
questions.ex: Gastrectomy removes the source of intrinsic factor, needed for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Unlike folate deficiency, B12 deficiency also causes neurologic dysfunction.

questions.q: Which antibacterial is commonly used to eradicate H. pylori?
questions.ex: Clarithromycin (with a PPI, ± amoxicillin/metronidazole/bismuth/tetracycline) is a mainstay of H. pylori eradication regimens.

questions.q: Perforation and inflammation of colonic diverticula
questions.ans: Diverticulitis

questions.q: Inflammation of the gallbladder, almost always accompanied by gallstones (chronic form)
questions.ans: Cholecystitis
questions.note: Cholelithiasis = stones in the gallbladder/biliary tree; cholecystitis = the inflammation, usually from obstruction.

questions.q: Released by gastric chief cells
questions.ans: Pepsinogen

questions.q: Toxic metabolite formed in acetaminophen-induced liver injury
questions.ans: NAPQI
questions.note: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine — normally detoxified by glutathione conjugation until GSH is depleted.

questions.q: Di/tripeptide transporter dependent on the H+ gradient from gut lumen to cell
questions.ans: PepT1

questions.q: GI endocrine hormone released by S cells of the duodenum
questions.ans: Secretin

questions.q: GI endocrine hormone released by I cells of the duodenum and jejunum
questions.ans: CCK (cholecystokinin)

questions.q: Gene mutated in familial adenomatous polyposis
questions.ans: APC

questions.q: Macrophages of the liver that phagocytose pathogens and old RBCs
questions.ans: Kupffer cells

questions.q: Bacterium causing pseudomembranous colitis after antibiotic-driven overgrowth
questions.ans: Clostridium difficile

questions.q: H2 receptor blocker available over the counter
questions.ans: Cimetidine

questions.q: IBD limited to the mucosal and submucosal layers of the colon
questions.ans: Ulcerative colitis

questions.q: Virus causing ~50% of acute hepatitis in the US, spread fecal-oral
questions.ans: Hepatitis A

questions.q: Virus spread by IV drug use and sexual contact, ~40% of acute US hepatitis cases
questions.ans: Hepatitis B

questions.q: Dopamine receptor antagonist used as an antiemetic for chemotherapy-associated nausea
questions.ans: Metoclopramide

questions.q: Intestinal cell type at the crypt base that secretes antimicrobials (lysozyme, defensins)
questions.ans: Paneth cells

questions.q: Delayed gastric emptying
questions.ans: Gastroparesis

questions.q: In Crohn's disease, the lesions are ___ (through the full bowel wall, with skip areas and granulomas)
questions.ans: Transmural

questions.q: Disease from a copper transporter (ATP7B) mutation, marked by the Kayser-Fleischer ring
questions.ans: Wilson disease

questions.q: Yellow skin pigmentation from high bilirubin
questions.ans: Jaundice

questions.q: Tonicity of the primary secretion from the small-intestine crypts (mainly NaCl)
questions.ans: Isotonic

questions.q: Esophageal carcinoma type associated with alcohol and tobacco use
questions.ans: Squamous cell carcinoma

questions.q: Fatty liver — triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes
questions.ans: Steatosis

questions.q: Required for micelle formation to transport fatty acids through an aqueous environment
questions.ans: Bile salts

questions.q: Autoimmune reaction to the gluten protein in wheat
questions.ans: Celiac disease

questions.q: Replacement of normal liver tissue with fibrotic scar tissue
questions.ans: Cirrhosis

questions.q: Structure at each corner of the classic hepatic lobule — portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct together
questions.ans: Portal triad

questions.q: Synthetic somatostatin analog used for short-gut/dumping-syndrome diarrhea
questions.ans: Octreotide

questions.q: Colon cancer type that is the 3rd most common cause of cancer death in the US
questions.ans: Adenocarcinoma

questions.q: Liver cell type that stores fat and vitamin A, sitting in the Space of Disse
questions.ans: Stellate (Ito) cells

questions.q: Most common form of esophagitis
questions.ans: GERD

questions.q: Permanent macroscopic folds of the small-intestine mucosa and submucosa
questions.ans: Plicae circulares
questions.note: Not the same as villi — microscopic finger-like projections of the mucosa alone.

questions.q: Presence of gallstones in the gallbladder
questions.ans: Cholelithiasis

questions.q: Syndrome caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor
questions.ans: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

questions.q: GI tumor arising from the gut's benign pacemaker cells (interstitial cells of Cajal)
questions.ans: GIST (GI stromal tumor)

questions.q: Opioid agonist with essentially no CNS penetration, widely used as an antidiarrheal
questions.ans: Loperamide

questions.q: Drug class defined by inhibiting the H+/K+-ATPase
questions.ans: Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole)

questions.q: GI paracrine that inhibits gastrin release
questions.ans: Somatostatin

questions.q: Metabolic liver disease causing iron accumulation in tissues
questions.ans: Hemochromatosis

questions.q: Most common type of gallstone
questions.ans: Cholesterol stones

questions.q: Most common liver disease in the US
questions.ans: Alcoholic liver disease

questions.q: Precancerous condition from chronic GERD — esophageal columnar metaplasia
questions.ans: Barrett's esophagus

questions.q: Which zone of the liver lobule is closest to the arterial (portal) supply?
questions.ex: Zone 1 (periportal) sits nearest the portal triad and gets the most oxygenated blood — it handles gluconeogenesis and ureagenesis. Zone 3 (perivenular) is most O2-poor and most vulnerable to ischemia. 84% of the class got this right in the live PollEverywhere review.

questions.q: Which liver injury pattern is NOT typical of acute hepatitis?
questions.ex: Bridging fibrosis reflects chronic, ongoing injury — a feature of chronic hepatitis, not the acute form. Only 25% of the class got this right live — one of the most commonly missed questions of the review.

questions.q: Which H2 blocker can cause gynecomastia from antiandrogenic effects?
questions.ex: Cimetidine carries more drug interactions and endocrine side effects (gynecomastia, impotence, galactorrhea) than famotidine. 52% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which statement about bile salts is correct?
ch: They are toxic to hepatocytes but not enterocytes
They are essential for micelle formation
They are synthesized only in the gallbladder
questions.ex: Bile salts are amphipathic detergents that solubilize dietary lipids into micelles — without them, fat absorption fails. Only 37% of the class got this right — commonly missed.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence for fat digestion and absorption?
ch: Bile coating → lipase action → micelle formation → absorption → chylomicron formation → lymphatic release
Lipase action → bile coating → absorption → micelle formation → lymphatic release → chylomicron formation
Micelle formation → bile coating → lipase action → chylomicron formation → absorption → lymphatic release
Bile coating → absorption → lipase action → micelle formation → chylomicron formation → lymphatic release
questions.ex: Bile coats and emulsifies fat, lipase/colipase digest it, the products form micelles that ferry them to the enterocyte, and inside the cell long-chain products are repackaged into chylomicrons for release into the lacteals. 55% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which GI cancer accounts for the highest number of deaths in the US?
questions.ex: Colorectal adenocarcinoma causes more GI-cancer deaths in the US than any other, per this course's material — though pancreatic cancer has a notably worse per-case mortality rate. 74% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which condition fits bulky, greasy stools and gluten sensitivity?
questions.ex: Celiac disease damages small-intestinal villi via an autoimmune reaction to gluten, causing fat malabsorption (steatorrhea) alongside the gluten trigger. 81% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which bacterium is most associated with chronic gastritis?
questions.ex: H. pylori colonizes the gastric mucosa and drives chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and gastric cancer risk. 93% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which intestinal cell type delivers luminal antigens to immune cells in Peyer's patches?
questions.ex: M (microfold) cells overlie Peyer's patches, endocytose luminal antigens, and hand them to lymphocytes waiting just beneath. 59% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Amiloride would impair intestinal absorption of:
questions.ex: PepT1-mediated di/tripeptide uptake depends on an inward H+ gradient maintained by Na+/H+ exchange; amiloride blocks that exchanger and collapses the gradient PepT1 needs — only 29% of the class got this right when it came up in the review session. Dr. Herr has since confirmed this specific question will NOT be on the actual exam, since this content wasn't covered for this class; kept here for reference only, and excluded from Mock Exam.

questions.q: Fat enters enterocytes primarily as:
questions.ex: Lipase/colipase break triglycerides down to free fatty acids and monoglycerides, which diffuse into the enterocyte — triglycerides are only re-synthesized after absorption. 49% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Gallbladder hypomotility leading to gallstones may result from:
questions.ex: CCK acting on CCK-A receptors is the main driver of gallbladder contraction after a fatty meal; losing that receptor leaves bile stagnant and prone to stone formation. 50% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which hormone combination most strongly stimulates pancreatic secretion?
questions.ex: Secretin, CCK, and ACh act synergistically — together they produce far more secretion than any single signal alone, conserving hormone. 44% of the class got this right.

questions.q: In a study, rats are given various acid stimulants. Which drug blocks acid secretion regardless of the stimulus?
questions.ex: PPIs act on the final common pathway — the H+/K+-ATPase itself — so they block acid output no matter which upstream signal (ACh, histamine, or gastrin) triggered it.

questions.q: A liver biopsy shows bile buildup in small channels. Through which structure does bile first flow from hepatocytes?
questions.ex: Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi between adjacent cells — not into the sinusoids/blood — which drain toward the canals of Hering and portal bile ducts. 55% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Which enzyme is NOT secreted by pancreatic acinar cells?
questions.ex: Pepsin(ogen) is a gastric product. Pancreatic acinar cells secrete amylase, lipases, nucleases, and protease zymogens. 67% of the class got this right.

questions.q: A history of pseudomembranous colitis points to overgrowth of:
questions.ex: C. difficile overgrowth (often post-antibiotic) produces toxins that cause the characteristic pseudomembranes. 60% of the class got this right.

questions.q: A patient with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome will most likely be prescribed:
questions.ex: PPIs like omeprazole are first-line for the massive acid hypersecretion driven by a gastrinoma. This was the best-answered pharmacology question in the live review — most of the class got it right.

questions.q: Which antiemetic acts on the vestibular system and blocks H1 receptors?
questions.ex: Meclizine is a first-generation H1 antihistamine used for motion sickness and vertigo. Scopolamine also treats motion sickness, but via muscarinic — not H1 — blockade. Only 34% of the class got this right — the antiemetic drug-class/mechanism pairings are easy to cross up.

questions.q: Which liver condition is most associated with metabolic syndrome?
questions.ex: NASH mimics alcoholic liver disease without alcohol use and is tightly linked to obesity, diabetes, and insulin resistance. 49% of the class got this right.

questions.q: Best initial treatment for mild Crohn's disease?
questions.ex: Corrected by the course director: methotrexate is the keyed answer, not sulfasalazine. This hub's own drug reference (drawn straight from the lecture transcript) draws the same line — methotrexate "induces and maintains remission in Crohn's disease," while sulfasalazine's entry is scoped to "mild-moderate ulcerative colitis" only. The original PollEverywhere session that day scored this question against sulfasalazine (just 29% of the class picked methotrexate) — that older key is now superseded.

questions.q: What is the 'metabolic unit of the liver' organized around blood flow from the portal triad to the central vein?
questions.ex: The classic lobule (Kiernan) is organized geometrically around the central vein; the acinus (Rappaport) reframes the same tissue around blood flow — portal triad (zone 1) to central vein (zone 3) — which is why zonation is described acinus-first.

questions.q: How do blood and lymph flow relative to each other in the liver?
ch: Blood flows portal → central; lymph flows central → portal (opposite directions)
Lymph and blood mix freely in the sinusoids
questions.ex: Blood moves portal triad → sinusoids → central vein. Lymph forms in the Space of Disse and flows the opposite way, toward portal-area lymphatics. Bile, blood, and lymph are each kept in their own separate channels — never mixed.

questions.q: Space between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium where plasma filtrate becomes hepatic lymph
questions.ans: Space of Disse
questions.note: Contains stellate (Ito) cells and collagen fibers; appears enlarged on some slide preps due to fixation shrinkage.

questions.q: How much can the gallbladder concentrate bile, and by what mechanism?
questions.ans: Up to ~10×, by absorbing water and electrolytes across its simple columnar epithelium
questions.note: It stores up to ~50 mL between meals and releases it via CCK-driven contraction plus sphincter of Oddi relaxation.

questions.q: Which liver zone handles most CYP450 drug/toxin biotransformation, making it most vulnerable to toxins like acetaminophen?
questions.ex: Zone 3 does the bulk of CYP450 oxidation and is also the most oxygen-poor zone — a combination that makes it the classic site of acetaminophen-induced centrilobular necrosis.

questions.q: Which of these is a Zone 1 (periportal), not Zone 3, function?
questions.ex: Zone 1, closest to oxygen-rich portal blood, favors oxidative/synthetic housekeeping work — gluconeogenesis, ureagenesis, cholesterol synthesis. Zone 3 favors glycolysis, lipogenesis, and detox chemistry.

questions.q: Antidote for acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity, and how it works
questions.ans: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
questions.note: Replenishes glutathione, binds NAPQI directly, and restores sulfation conjugation — most protective within 8–10 hours of ingestion.

questions.q: The three phases of hepatic drug/hormone biotransformation, in order, are:
questions.ex: Phase I (oxidation, via CYP450) often comes first and can activate or even toxify a drug; Phase II (conjugation — glucuronidation is most common) boosts water solubility; Phase III eliminates the conjugate into blood or bile.

questions.q: How long can the liver's vitamin B12 stores prevent deficiency symptoms?
questions.ans: About 1–5 years
questions.note: This is why pernicious anemia or post-gastrectomy B12 malabsorption can take years to become symptomatic.

questions.q: What triggers secretin release from duodenal S cells?
questions.ex: Acid reaching the duodenum — and physiologically, fatty acids — trigger secretin, which drives pancreatic and biliary HCO3- secretion to neutralize that acid.

questions.q: Approximate size of the bile acid pool, and how many times per day it recycles
questions.ans: ~3 g pool, recycled 4–12 times per day
questions.note: That recycling lets a small pool deliver 12–36 g of bile acids to the gut daily — only ~0.2–0.6 g/day is newly synthesized to replace what's lost in stool.

questions.q: Bilirubin is converted in the gut to urobilinogen, most of which is:
ch: Reabsorbed and fully excreted by the kidney
Oxidized to urobilin/stercobilin and excreted, with some recirculated to the liver
questions.ex: Deconjugated bilirubin becomes colorless urobilinogen; most oxidizes to urobilin (colors urine) and stercobilin (colors stool), with a portion recirculated to the liver.

questions.q: Glucose and galactose cross the intestinal brush border via:
questions.ex: SGLT1 co-transports glucose/galactose with Na+ down the Na+ gradient (maintained by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase). Fructose instead crosses via facilitated diffusion through GLUT5.

questions.q: The three forms in which digested protein is absorbed by enterocytes
questions.ans: Free amino acids (Na+-dependent), di/tripeptides (H+-dependent via PepT1), and — minor — whole proteins by phagocytosis

questions.q: Where do chylomicrons go after leaving the enterocyte by exocytosis?
questions.ans: Into lacteals (lymphatics) of the villi, bypassing the liver to enter systemic circulation via the thoracic duct
questions.note: Unlike short/medium-chain fatty acids, which pass directly into the portal vein.

questions.q: Which drug class is most associated with acute dystonia, akathisia, and — rarely — neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
questions.ex: D2 antagonists like metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and droperidol block dopamine in the extrapyramidal tract, producing a time-dependent cascade of movement side effects.

questions.q: First-line quadruple therapy for H. pylori eradication
questions.ans: PPI + metronidazole + bismuth + tetracycline

questions.q: A patient on a PPI for years develops glossitis and mild anemia. Most likely cause?
questions.ex: Long-term PPI use is a recognized cause of B12 deficiency (along with magnesium deficiency and increased enteric infection risk), since acid suppression impairs B12 release from food.

questions.q: Antifolate IBD drug that inhibits DHFR and thymidylate synthase, and its classic side effect
questions.ans: Methotrexate — causes mucositis/stomatitis, eased by folic acid supplementation
questions.note: Also a teratogen/abortifacient — a key counseling point.

questions.q: Which oral finding is a classic early sign of liver disease, often visible before jaundice is obvious elsewhere?
questions.ex: Icteric sclera and oral mucosal jaundice are frequently the first visible sign of hyperbilirubinemia — worth checking before ordering labs.

questions.q: Before an invasive dental procedure on a patient with cirrhosis, which labs matter most?
questions.ex: Cirrhosis reduces synthesis of clotting factors and can cause thrombocytopenia (from splenomegaly/portal hypertension) — both raise bleeding risk during procedures.

questions.q: Two drug classes requiring caution before dental extractions because of osteonecrosis-of-the-jaw risk
questions.ans: Bisphosphonates and denosumab
questions.note: MRONJ risk — favor atraumatic technique and, where possible, treatment before starting the medication.

questions.q: Which small-intestine segment is distinguished by Brunner's glands secreting alkaline mucus (pH 8.1–9.3)?
questions.ex: Brunner's glands, in the duodenal submucosa, neutralize acidic chyme arriving from the stomach — unique to the duodenum.

questions.q: Which structure distinguishes the ileum histologically from the jejunum?
questions.ex: Peyer's patches — aggregated lymphoid nodules — mark the ileum. Plicae and crypts occur throughout the small intestine, just diminishing distally.

questions.q: Two external landmarks that distinguish large intestine from small intestine
questions.ans: Teniae coli (three longitudinal muscle bands) and haustra (sacculations)
questions.note: The colon also lacks plicae circulares and villi — its mucosal surface is smooth, with straight crypts only.

questions.q: By how much do plicae, villi, and microvilli together amplify small-intestinal absorptive surface area?
questions.ex: The three levels of folding stack multiplicatively — roughly 600-fold versus a flat tube, which is most of why the small intestine can absorb an entire day's nutrients.

questions.q: Put the steps of dietary fat digestion and absorption in order.
steps: Bile salts emulsify fat droplets in the duodenum
Pancreatic lipase + colipase digest triglycerides at the droplet surface
Fatty acids and monoglycerides are packaged into micelles
Micelle contents diffuse into the enterocyte
Long-chain products are re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons
Chylomicrons exit by exocytosis into the lacteals

questions.q: Put bile's path from hepatocyte to duodenum in order.
steps: Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi
Canaliculi drain into the canals of Hering
Canals of Hering feed intrahepatic bile ducts
Intrahepatic ducts join into the common hepatic duct
The cystic duct adds gallbladder bile, forming the common bile duct
The common bile duct joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla and empties into the duodenum

questions.q: Put the mechanism of acetaminophen (APAP) hepatotoxicity in order.
steps: Therapeutic APAP is mostly conjugated safely (glucuronidation/sulfation)
In overdose, more APAP is shunted through CYP450 oxidation
CYP450 oxidation generates the reactive metabolite NAPQI
Glutathione (GSH), which normally neutralizes NAPQI, becomes depleted
NAPQI covalently binds mitochondrial proteins and ion channels
Mitochondrial dysfunction and ATP depletion cause hepatocyte necrosis

questions.q: Put the extrapyramidal symptom (EPS) timeline for D2-antagonist antiemetics in order, soonest to latest.
steps: Acute dystonia (hours–days) — muscle spasms, oculogyric crisis
Akathisia (days) — restlessness, can't sit still
Parkinsonism (weeks–months) — rigidity, tremor
Tardive dyskinesia (months+) — involuntary movements, often irreversible

questions.q: Match the drug-name ending to its class.
Match each drug mechanism to its hallmark adverse effect.
Match the liver lobule zone to what happens there.
pairs: CYP450 detox, lipogenesis — lowest O2, most vulnerable

questions.q: Match each hepatitis virus to its key feature.
pairs: Blood/sexual/perinatal spread, dsDNA virus, vaccine available
Defective virus — needs HBsAg from Hepatitis B to infect
Fecal-oral, usually mild — except severe in pregnancy

questions.q: Match the type of jaundice to its cause.
Which pancreatic acinar cell product is secreted already ACTIVE, rather than as an inactive zymogen?
questions.ex: The proteases (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidases, procolipase) are secreted as inactive zymogens to protect the pancreas from autodigestion. Amylase, lipase, RNase, and DNase carry no such digestive risk to pancreatic tissue and are secreted already active.

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of duodenal HCO3- comes from the pancreas versus from duodenal surface cells?
ch: Entirely from surface cells; the pancreas contributes none
questions.ex: Bicarbonate secreted in response to duodenal acidity comes mostly from the pancreas (~60%), with the remaining ~40% from HCO3--secreting duodenal surface cells.

questions.q: What fraction of total pancreatic fluid volume originates from the duct cells rather than the acinar cells?
ch: Acinar cells produce all pancreatic fluid
questions.ex: Although acinar cells make the enzymes, the bulk of pancreatic fluid VOLUME (80-90%) is generated by duct cells secreting water and NaHCO3 — a classic exam distinction between who makes the enzymes and who makes the fluid.

questions.q: Approximate daily volume of pancreatic fluid secretion
questions.ans: 1-2.5 liters/day
questions.note: Composed largely of water and NaHCO3; the Cl-:HCO3- secretion ratio varies inversely as flow rate increases.

questions.q: Put the three neural phases of pancreatic secretion in order, with their key trigger.
steps: Cephalic phase — vagal efferents act directly on acinar cells and ducts (~10% of secretion)
Gastric phase — gastric distension triggers a vagovagal reflex to the pancreas
Intestinal phase — duodenal afferents respond to digestion products via a vagovagal reflex

questions.q: Why does the body store and concentrate bile acids in a gallbladder rather than secreting them continuously?
questions.ans: Bile acids are powerful detergents that are also toxic amphipaths to enterocytes, get lost with rapid transit, and are modified by gut bacteria — so the body 'bags' them (gallbladder), concentrates the bag to keep it small, coats it in protective mucus, and releases the contents only under neurohumoral control (CCK) when a meal actually needs them.
questions.note: A good way to remember this as a 'why' question, not just a 'what' — bile acid storage solves a problem bile acids create for themselves.

questions.q: Bile acids returning to the liver via the portal circulation have what effect on the hepatocyte?
ch: They stimulate further bile acid synthesis
They inhibit further bile acid synthesis, while still stimulating bile flow
They have no effect on hepatocyte function
They are immediately destroyed by Kupffer cells
questions.ex: Recirculating bile acids act as their own negative-feedback signal — they inhibit new bile acid synthesis in hepatocytes even as they stimulate ongoing bile flow. This is why interrupting the enterohepatic circulation forces the liver to ramp up new synthesis.

questions.q: What are bile acids conjugated to before secretion, and what does this accomplish?
questions.ans: Taurine and glycine — conjugation alters the bile acid's pKa, keeping it ionized (and a more effective detergent) across the pH range found in the gut

questions.q: CCK's coordinated effect on the biliary tree during a fatty meal is to:
ch: Contract the gallbladder and contract the sphincter of Oddi
Relax the gallbladder and relax the sphincter of Oddi
Contract the gallbladder and relax the sphincter of Oddi
Relax the gallbladder and contract the sphincter of Oddi
questions.ex: CCK squeezes bile out of the gallbladder while simultaneously opening the gate (relaxing the sphincter of Oddi) — the two effects have to happen together for bile to actually reach the duodenum.

questions.q: How does the pancreas's HCO3- secretion rate relate to duodenal pH and to overall flow rate?
questions.ans: HCO3- secretion rises as duodenal pH falls (more acid drives a bigger bicarbonate response) and rises with increasing flow rate (higher secretory rates favor HCO3- over Cl- in the ductal fluid)

questions.q: Before hepatic uptake, unconjugated bilirubin travels through the blood bound to:
questions.ex: Bilirubin from heme breakdown is poorly water-soluble and is carried through plasma bound to albumin until the liver actively extracts and conjugates it to glucuronide.

questions.q: Pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, and elastase are all classified as endopeptidases. What does this mean, in contrast to an exopeptidase like carboxypeptidase?
ch: Endopeptidases only work inside the stomach
Endopeptidases cleave internal peptide bonds within a protein chain; exopeptidases cleave bonds only at the chain's terminal end
Endopeptidases require no activation; exopeptidases always do
questions.ex: Endopeptidases cut internal bonds, fragmenting a large protein into smaller pieces; exopeptidases (carboxypeptidase A and B) then trim residues off the free end of those fragments — the two classes work together to fully break a protein down.

questions.q: Beyond activating itself, what other pancreatic zymogens does trypsin activate once formed?
questions.ans: Chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin, proelastase → elastase, and procarboxypeptidase A/B → carboxypeptidase A/B — trypsin sits at the top of a proteolytic activation cascade
questions.note: This is why enteropeptidase deficiency (which normally makes the first trypsin) cripples digestion of essentially all dietary protein, not just one enzyme's worth.

questions.q: Gastric lipase (optimal pH ~4.0) contributes roughly what share of total fat digestion?
questions.ex: Gastric lipase (plus a small lingual lipase contribution) handles roughly 10-30% of fat digestion before food ever reaches the duodenum — most of the work is still done by pancreatic lipase, but the gastric phase isn't negligible.

questions.q: Bile salts coating a fat droplet create a specific problem for pancreatic lipase. What is it, and how does colipase solve it?
ch: Bile salts destroy lipase directly; colipase regenerates it
Bile salts displace lipase off the droplet surface; colipase stabilizes lipase's interaction with the bile-salt-coated droplet, letting it keep working
Bile salts activate lipase for the first time; colipase is not needed afterward
Bile salts have no interaction with lipase
questions.ex: Bile salts are needed to emulsify fat but, as a side effect, they also displace lipase from the droplet surface. Colipase anchors lipase back onto the bile-salt-coated droplet — solving the very problem bile salts created.

questions.q: After absorption into the enterocyte, how do short/medium-chain fatty acids differ from long-chain fatty acids in their onward route?
ch: Both are packaged into chylomicrons and enter lymphatics
Short/medium-chain fatty acids pass directly into the portal vein; long-chain fatty acids are re-esterified to triglycerides, packaged into chylomicrons, and enter the lymphatics via lacteals
Both pass directly into the portal vein
Short-chain fatty acids are not absorbed at all
questions.ex: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are small/water-soluble enough to diffuse directly into the portal circulation, bypassing the chylomicron/lymphatic pathway — only long-chain fatty acids and monoglycerides need repackaging into chylomicrons.

questions.q: What is the dominant component of a chylomicron by weight?
questions.ans: Triglyceride (~90%)
questions.note: The rest is mostly phospholipid (~6.5%) with smaller shares of cholesterol ester, free cholesterol, and apolipoprotein coat protein.

questions.q: What fraction of ingested dietary lipid is triglyceride, as opposed to phospholipid, cholesterol, or fat-soluble vitamins?
questions.ex: About 90% of dietary lipid is triglyceride — the remainder is phospholipids, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which still require the same bile-salt/micelle system to be absorbed.

questions.q: Roughly how many grams of protein, fat, and carbohydrate are in a 200 g Big Mac (this lecture's illustrative example), and roughly how many total calories?
questions.ans: ~25 g protein, ~28 g fat, ~47 g carbohydrate, ~530 Calories
questions.note: Used to illustrate that the patties/cheese supply protein and fat, the bun supplies starch, and the lettuce/pickles/onion supply mostly indigestible cellulose plus a little starch.

questions.q: Where does absorption of the products of fat digestion occur?
questions.ex: Unlike bile salt reabsorption or B12 absorption (both specifically terminal ileum), absorption of lipolytic products happens throughout the length of the small intestine.

questions.q: Where does lipid digestion/emulsification physiologically begin, before any bile salts are involved?
questions.ans: The mouth (lingual lipase, a small contribution) and the stomach (gastric lipase, plus mechanical grinding, stabilized by phospholipids acting as emulsifiers)

questions.q: The liver is considered both what two organ types simultaneously?
questions.ans: An endocrine AND an exocrine organ — endocrine via direct secretion of plasma proteins/clotting factors into blood, exocrine via bile secretion into the biliary tree

questions.q: Beyond its more familiar metabolic roles, the liver also performs which hormone-processing function?
ch: Converts T3 to the active T4 form
Converts thyroid hormone T4 to the active T3 form
questions.ex: A notable and easy-to-forget hepatic job: peripheral conversion of T4 to the more biologically active T3.

questions.q: Name a liver-secreted glycoprotein (besides transferrin) involved in iron transport
questions.ans: Haptoglobin
questions.note: Haptoglobin specifically binds free hemoglobin released by hemolysis, while transferrin transports free iron — both liver products, both iron-pathway related.

questions.q: Match each fluid to its dedicated hepatic channel — remember, the three never mix.
pairs: Canaliculi → bile ducts (mixing with blood causes jaundice)
Space of Disse → portal lymphatics (flows opposite to blood)

questions.q: Which layer(s) of the typical GI tract wall does the gallbladder characteristically LACK?
questions.ex: Unlike most of the GI tract, the gallbladder lacks a distinct submucosa and muscularis mucosae — its mucosal folds sit directly on connective tissue next to the muscularis externa. A classic identifying histology feature.

questions.q: Approximate gallbladder dimensions per this lecture
questions.ans: Pear-shaped muscular sac, 7-10 cm long

questions.q: Gallbladder epithelial cells contain unusually large concentrations of mitochondria in their apical and basal cytoplasm. What does this reflect functionally?
ch: The active Na+ transport that drives water reabsorption to concentrate bile
Bile acid synthesis occurring in the epithelium itself
questions.ex: Concentrating bile up to 10-fold requires actively pumping Na+ (water follows) — an energy-hungry process, hence the mitochondria-dense epithelium with microvilli and lateral plications that further increase transport surface area.

questions.q: Location and approximate dimensions of the pancreas, per this histology lecture
questions.ans: Posterior abdominal wall, mostly retroperitoneal; about 12-15 cm long, 4 cm wide, 2 cm thick

questions.q: Pancreatic acinar cells secrete a trypsin inhibitor alongside trypsinogen. What is the purpose of this?
ch: To slow overall enzyme output during fasting
To protect the pancreas from autodigestion if a small amount of trypsinogen is prematurely activated inside the gland
questions.ex: Trypsin inhibitor is a safety mechanism — it neutralizes any trypsin that activates prematurely inside the pancreas itself, helping prevent autodigestion/pancreatitis.

questions.q: Which duct/gland structures are notably ABSENT from the pancreas, distinguishing it from salivary glands despite both being compound acinar glands?
questions.ex: Pancreatic acini contain centroacinar cells (unique to the pancreas) but — unlike salivary glands — lack striated ducts and myoepithelial cells. A useful distinguishing point if a slide could otherwise pass for either gland.

questions.q: Besides mucosal plasma cells, what OTHER route delivers secretory IgA to the intestinal lumen?
questions.ans: Bile — one of bile's listed functions is transporting IgA to the intestinal mucosa, in addition to IgA secreted directly by plasma cells in the gut wall itself
questions.note: Connects this lecture to the intestinal histology lecture — IgA reaches the gut by two independent routes.

questions.q: A hepatocyte secretes bile into the canaliculus and extracts/secretes plasma proteins at the sinusoidal surface. This describes:
ch: A single, non-polarized surface performing both functions
Polarized function — a distinct apical (canalicular) surface for bile secretion and a distinct basolateral (sinusoidal) surface for blood-facing exchange
Random distribution of both functions across the whole membrane
Function that alternates over time rather than by location
questions.ex: Hepatocytes are polarized epithelial cells: the canalicular (apical) membrane secretes bile, while the sinusoidal (basolateral) membrane handles uptake/secretion into and from plasma — one cell, two faces, two jobs.

questions.q: Beyond emulsifying fat, name two other functions of bile listed in this lecture
questions.ans: Excretion route for cholesterol, phospholipids, bile salts, conjugated bilirubin, electrolytes, and drug/toxin metabolites; and an antibacterial action that inhibits intestinal bacterial overgrowth (in addition to transporting IgA to the mucosa)

questions.q: Gallbladder emptying is triggered by which combination of signals?
ch: Both CCK (hormonal) and vagal (neural) stimulation of contraction
questions.ex: Gallbladder contraction has both a hormonal driver (CCK, released in response to duodenal fat) and a neural driver (vagal stimulation) — redundant control for a function that needs to fire reliably after every fatty meal.

questions.q: Approximate length of each small intestine segment: duodenum, jejunum, ileum
questions.ans: Duodenum ~25 cm, jejunum ~2.5 m, ileum ~3.5 m
questions.note: The jejunum and ileum together make up the vast majority of small intestine length, even though the duodenum gets disproportionate lecture time for its unique landmarks.

questions.q: Which small intestine segment is histologically defined mainly by what it LACKS — neither Brunner's glands nor Peyer's patches?
questions.ex: The jejunum is the 'boring middle child' histologically: no Brunner's glands (that's the duodenum) and no aggregated Peyer's patches (that's the ileum) — often recognized by process of elimination.

questions.q: What structure binds adjacent enterocytes together near their apical margins, separating the intestinal lumen from the intercellular space?
questions.ex: Tight junctions seal the space between adjacent enterocytes near their luminal surface, creating the barrier that keeps luminal contents from freely entering intercellular/subepithelial spaces.

questions.q: How does goblet cell density change along the length of the small intestine?
questions.ans: Goblet cells increase in number from the duodenum to the ileum
questions.note: The same gradient continues into the colon, which has even more goblet cells — more mucus is needed as luminal contents become more solid/bacteria-laden distally.

questions.q: How do Paneth cell defensins exert their antimicrobial effect?
ch: They increase target-organism membrane permeability by forming ion channels
questions.ex: Defensins are small antimicrobial peptides that insert into and permeabilize the membranes of target bacteria/parasites by forming ion channels — distinct from lysozyme, which degrades the bacterial peptidoglycan coat.

questions.q: Name the antimicrobial substances secreted by Paneth cells, and how lysozyme specifically works
questions.ans: Lysozyme and defensins (antimicrobial glycoproteins); lysozyme increases bacterial membrane permeability by degrading their peptidoglycan coat
questions.note: Paneth cells increase in number during certain infections/conditions, and TNF-alpha is produced locally in response to infectious agents and tissue injury.

questions.q: Enteroendocrine cells are considered part of the 'DNES.' What does this stand for, and what does it imply about their secretions?
ch: Digestive Neural Excretory System — secretions act only within the gut lumen
Diffuse NeuroEndocrine System — their peptides can have both endocrine (bloodstream) AND paracrine (local) effects
Dual Nerve Enteric System — purely neural signaling, no hormone release
Dorsal Neuroendocrine Structure — a CNS classification, not a gut one
questions.ex: Enteroendocrine cells are scattered (diffuse) throughout the gut and belong to the same broad neuroendocrine cell family found elsewhere in the body — their peptides can act at a distance (endocrine) or locally (paracrine); not every secreted peptide even reaches the lumen.

questions.q: Exact pH range of the alkaline mucus/bicarbonate secretion from Brunner's glands
What are the large intestine's primary functions, given that it performs essentially no enzymatic digestion?
ch: Active absorption of electrolytes and water, plus moving and storing waste until evacuation
questions.ex: Having no villi (and much less enzymatic machinery than the small intestine), the colon's job is mainly active electrolyte/water reabsorption from remaining chyme, plus propelling and storing the resulting waste.

questions.q: What immune-related feature distinguishes the appendix histologically, and what other cell type's presence confirms its role in host defense?
questions.ans: A large number of lymphatic nodules extending into the submucosa; Paneth cells are also present, reinforcing its immune role

questions.q: Moving distally through the anal canal, the epithelium transitions in which order?
ch: Stratified squamous → simple columnar → keratinized skin
Simple columnar → stratified squamous → keratinized (skin-like) near the anal opening
Keratinized skin → simple columnar → stratified squamous
Simple columnar throughout, with no transition
questions.ex: The rectal mucosa (simple columnar, like the rest of the colon) transitions to stratified squamous at the anorectal junction, then becomes keratinized near the anal opening as it blends into true skin — three zones sometimes labeled CRZ, ATZ, and SQZ.

questions.q: What glandular structures are present in the anal canal submucosa?
questions.ans: Anal glands

questions.q: M cells overlying Peyer's patches sample luminal antigen by which mechanism?
ch: Endocytosing luminal proteins and discharging the contents into the adjacent extracellular space, where lymphocytes respond to the antigen
Direct phagocytosis of whole bacteria only
Secretion of antibodies into the lumen
questions.ex: M cells endocytose (rather than digest) luminal antigens and deliver them into the extracellular space just beneath, where resident lymphocytes are positioned to respond — a transport/delivery role rather than a digestive one.

questions.q: Why does dietary cellulose (e.g., lettuce) pass through the GI tract largely unabsorbed?
ch: It is actively pumped out of enterocytes
Humans lack enzymes capable of breaking its glycosidic bonds, so it can't be digested to absorbable monosaccharides
It is too large to enter the mouth of a crypt
Cellulose is toxic and is actively excluded
questions.ex: Cellulose is a glucose polymer, but its bond configuration isn't cleaved by any human digestive enzyme — a reminder that 'made of glucose' doesn't guarantee digestibility. This makes it dietary fiber rather than an absorbable carbohydrate.

questions.q: Approximately how often does the small intestinal epithelium fully turn over, regenerating from crypt stem cells?
ch: It does not regenerate after birth
questions.ex: Villus epithelial cells turn over roughly every 3-5 days, continuously replaced by proliferating stem cells at the crypt base — which is also why rapidly-dividing crypt cells are especially vulnerable to chemotherapy/radiation, producing mucositis.

questions.q: What cytoskeletal element runs through each intestinal microvillus?
questions.ans: Contractile microfilaments — they help stabilize the brush border during the mechanical stress of digestion

questions.q: On a histology slide, straight tubular crypts with NO villi and NO plicae circulares identify the tissue as:
questions.ex: The colon retains crypts (for epithelial renewal and mucus output) but has no villi and no plicae circulares — a smooth mucosal surface is one of the fastest ways to identify large intestine on a slide.

questions.q: What structure delivers both bile and pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum?
questions.ans: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater)

questions.q: Enteroendocrine cells of the small intestine are localized primarily to which structure?
questions.ex: Enteroendocrine cells localize to the intestinal crypts (glands), alongside the stem, Paneth, and differentiating absorptive/goblet cells that also populate that compartment.

questions.q: The liver's functions are often grouped into five categories — name them
questions.ans: Exocrine (bile secretion), Endocrine (e.g. clotting factor secretion), Metabolic (e.g. fat metabolism), Storage (glycogen, iron, vitamins), and Protection (detoxification, Kupffer cells)

questions.q: Which clotting factor is notably NOT synthesized by the liver, unlike the rest of the classic coagulation cascade?
questions.ex: Factor VIII is made mainly by vascular endothelial cells, not hepatocytes — a classic exception worth memorizing, since severe liver disease does not reliably lower Factor VIII the way it lowers II, VII, IX, and X.

questions.q: Name the liver-secreted plasma carrier proteins for iron and for copper
questions.ans: Transferrin carries iron; ceruloplasmin carries copper

questions.q: Roughly how much glycogen does the liver store, and what enzyme — absent from brain and muscle — lets the liver (but not muscle) release that glycogen as free glucose into the blood?
questions.ex: The liver stores ~80 g of glycogen. Only the liver expresses glucose-6-phosphatase, which strips the phosphate so glucose can leave the cell — muscle glycogen lacks this enzyme and can only fuel the muscle cell itself, never raise blood glucose directly.

questions.q: Gluconeogenesis exists mainly to protect blood glucose for tissues that obligately depend on it. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.ex: RBCs (no mitochondria), renal medulla, cornea/lens, and brain are classic obligate glucose users. Resting skeletal muscle runs comfortably on fatty acids and doesn't need gluconeogenesis to protect its glucose supply the way these tissues do.

questions.q: What single intermediate must all non-carbohydrate gluconeogenic precursors (lactate, pyruvate, TCA intermediates, amino acid carbon chains) be converted to before entering the gluconeogenic pathway?
questions.ans: Oxaloacetate

questions.q: In the FED state, where does glucose UPTAKE into hepatocytes occur first?
ch: Uptake is uniform across all zones
questions.ex: Blood (and its glucose) enters at the portal triad, so Zone 1 sees it first and is first to take it up for glycogen synthesis/glycolysis in the fed state. In fasting, the same zone releases glucose first, for the same reason — it's the first stop for whatever the blood is carrying.

questions.q: Name the two enzyme systems the liver uses to clear ammonia, and how their capacity/affinity differ
questions.ans: Carbamoyl phosphate synthase (CPS) in Zone 1 — high capacity, low affinity, drives urea synthesis; glutamine synthase (GS) in Zone 3 — low capacity, high affinity, mops up ammonia that escapes Zone 1
questions.note: Often described as a 'safety net': the high-volume Zone 1 pathway handles most ammonia, and the high-affinity Zone 3 pathway catches what's left before it reaches systemic circulation.

questions.q: What is the major source of the ammonia that reaches portal blood?
ch: Direct hepatocyte production during protein synthesis
Bacterial breakdown of unabsorbed protein/amino acids in the intestine, followed by bacterial ureases converting urea to ammonia
questions.ex: The intestine is the major contributor: bacterial proteases break down unabsorbed dietary protein and bacterial ureases then convert the resulting urea to ammonia, which diffuses freely into the portal circulation for the liver to detoxify.

questions.q: Statins lower cholesterol synthesis by inhibiting which hepatic enzyme?
questions.ex: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis — and the direct target of statin drugs.

questions.q: Which is the most common Phase II conjugation reaction in hepatic drug metabolism?
questions.ex: Glucuronic acid conjugation, catalyzed by glucuronyl transferases, is by far the most common Phase II reaction — alongside less common sulfate, acetyl, methyl, and glutathione conjugation, all aimed at increasing water solubility for excretion.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches a CYP450 inducer with a CYP450 inhibitor?
questions.ex: Phenobarbital (and cigarette smoke) induce Phase I CYP450 enzymes, speeding drug metabolism; cimetidine inhibits Phase I enzymes, prolonging the half-life of co-administered drugs — opposite ends of the same enzyme system.

questions.q: Why are IV drug doses typically much lower than oral doses of the same medication?
questions.ans: The 'first-pass effect' — orally absorbed drugs are extensively metabolized by the liver (and to some extent the enterocyte) before ever reaching systemic circulation, reducing bioavailability. IV doses skip this first pass entirely.
questions.note: Albumin binding of circulating drug can further limit bioavailability, independent of hepatic metabolism.

questions.q: Per this lecture, what single acute dose of acetaminophen can produce potentially fatal hepatic necrosis?
questions.ex: Therapeutic dosing (1-4 g/day) is safe, but a single acute overdose above roughly 10-15 g can cause fatal hepatic necrosis — and chronic dosing as low as 4-6 g/day can also be fatal over time, which is the more easily overlooked danger.

questions.q: At therapeutic doses, what fraction of acetaminophen is safely conjugated (Phase II) versus oxidized by CYP450 to NAPQI?
questions.ans: ~95% safely conjugated (glucuronidation/sulfation); only ~5% goes through CYP450 oxidation to NAPQI
questions.note: In overdose, the conjugation pathways saturate and a larger share gets shunted through CYP450 to NAPQI — which is what overwhelms glutathione stores.

questions.q: N-acetylcysteine given within 8-10 hours of an acetaminophen overdose provides roughly what level of protection against liver injury?
questions.ex: NAC is dramatically time-sensitive: ~90% protection within 8-10 hours, dropping to ~40-70% by 10-24 hours. It's still given later than that, but with rapidly diminishing benefit — which is why early recognition of overdose matters so much.

questions.q: Why does a disproportionate rise in AST relative to ALT suggest more severe (e.g., mitochondrial) hepatocyte injury, such as in alcoholic hepatitis?
ch: AST is cytosolic and leaks out with minor injury; ALT is mitochondrial and needs severe injury
ALT is cytosolic and leaks out with minor injury; AST is also cytosolic but less liver-specific
ALT is cytosolic (leaks with any injury); AST is partly mitochondrial (needs more severe injury to release)
AST and ALT are both mitochondrial and rise together
questions.ex: ALT sits in the cytosol and leaks out with even mild hepatocyte injury. AST is partly mitochondrial, so a disproportionate AST rise (classically AST:ALT > 2 in alcoholic liver disease) implies injury severe enough to damage mitochondria, not just the cell membrane.

questions.q: Which vitamin has the SHORTEST hepatic storage reserve, making deficiency appear soonest after intake stops?
ch: All three deplete at the same rate
questions.ex: Vitamin D reserves (~3-4 months) run out fastest, then vitamin A (~10 months), with B12 stores lasting years — which is why B12 deficiency from causes like gastrectomy or strict veganism can take a surprisingly long time to become symptomatic.

questions.q: Trace vitamin D's activation pathway from the skin to its most active form
questions.ans: Skin makes cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) → the liver converts it to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol → the kidney converts that to 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol), the most active form
questions.note: Two-organ activation — liver first, then kidney — is why both hepatic and renal disease can each independently cause vitamin D-deficient states.

questions.q: Ethanol metabolism at blood levels above ~100 mg/dL increasingly relies on a 'back-up' oxidation pathway once the primary route saturates. This describes:
ch: Zero-order kinetics throughout the entire range, with no saturation ever occurring
A primary pathway that saturates at higher ethanol concentrations, recruiting a secondary microsomal (CYP2E1-based) route to handle the excess
Complete renal clearance of ethanol at high concentrations
A pathway that only activates at very low ethanol concentrations
questions.ex: Alcohol dehydrogenase handles ethanol efficiently at lower concentrations but saturates around 100 mg/dL; above that, the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (CYP2E1-based) increasingly takes over — the same enzyme implicated in acetaminophen's NAPQI pathway, part of why chronic drinkers are more vulnerable to APAP hepatotoxicity.

questions.q: How does 'fibrosis' differ from 'cirrhosis' in this lecture's terminology?
ch: They are interchangeable terms for the same finding
Fibrosis is ECM deposition localized around the peri-sinusoidal space/portal tracts; cirrhosis is exaggerated ECM deposition forming interconnected bands of scar tissue
Fibrosis only occurs in Zone 1; cirrhosis only in Zone 3
Cirrhosis is reversible; fibrosis is not
questions.ex: Fibrosis is the earlier, more localized ECM deposition around portal tracts/central veins; cirrhosis is the advanced, diffuse, interconnected scarring that replaces normal architecture — fibrosis can be an early, sometimes-reversible step on the way toward irreversible cirrhosis.

questions.q: What activates the normally quiescent, vitamin-A-storing stellate (Ito) cell into a collagen-producing myofibroblast?
ch: Hepatocyte injury (e.g., free radicals from alcohol metabolism), triggering TGF-β1 secretion and matrix remodeling by the stellate cell
questions.ex: Hepatocyte injury — such as free radical generation during alcohol detoxification — activates stellate cells into myofibroblast-like cells that secrete TGF-β1, lay down collagen, and increase metalloproteinase-driven matrix turnover, disrupting blood flow and driving fibrosis/cirrhosis.

questions.q: Both HMG-CoA reductase (cholesterol synthesis) and cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (bile acid synthesis) are concentrated in which liver zone?
questions.ans: Zone 1 (periportal)
questions.note: A useful 'trick' pairing — both major cholesterol-handling enzymes sit in Zone 1, even though bile acid synthesis might intuitively feel like more of a Zone 3 'detox' job.

questions.q: What fraction of the liver's blood supply comes from the portal vein rather than the hepatic artery?
questions.ex: The portal vein supplies ~65% of hepatic blood flow (nutrient-rich, low-O2) and the hepatic artery ~35% (oxygen-rich) — together the two inflows make up about 25% of total cardiac output.

questions.q: Approximate weight and location of the liver, per this lecture
questions.ans: 1400–1600 g, right upper quadrant (~2.5% of body weight)
questions.note: Spans roughly the right 5th intercostal space down to just below the costal margin.

questions.q: Match each liver lab test category to what it reflects.
Why does prothrombin time (PT) rise in liver failure?
ch: Reduced synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X
questions.ex: The liver synthesizes the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X); failing synthetic function shows up first as a prolonged PT/INR.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of liver function must be lost before hepatic failure develops?
questions.ex: The liver's functional reserve is large — clinical hepatic failure typically doesn't appear until 80-90% of function is lost.

questions.q: List the classic clinical features of hepatic failure beyond jaundice and coagulopathy
questions.ans: Hypoalbuminemia, hyperammonemia/hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, fetor hepaticus, palmar erythema, spider angiomata, hypogonadism
questions.note: These follow from the liver's lost synthetic (albumin, clotting factors), detox (ammonia), and hormone-clearance (estrogen buildup → spider angiomata, palmar erythema, hypogonadism) functions.

questions.q: A patient has Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein obstruction) causing portal hypertension. This is classified as:
questions.ex: Portal hypertension is staged like jaundice: prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (liver disease itself), and posthepatic (Budd-Chiari/hepatic vein or outflow obstruction).

questions.q: Minimum duration of hepatitis before it's classified as 'chronic'
questions.ans: 6 months

questions.q: Match each variable immune response pattern in viral hepatitis to its outcome.
Which statement about Hepatitis A virus is correct?
ch: Enveloped dsDNA virus that commonly becomes chronic
Nonenveloped RNA picornavirus with no chronic infection
Spread parenterally with an 85% chronicity rate
Defective virus requiring HBsAg for infection
questions.ex: HAV is a nonenveloped RNA picornavirus, fecal-oral spread, ~28-day incubation, causing ~50% of US acute hepatitis — and unlike B, C, or D, it never becomes chronic.

questions.q: Per this lecture, what fraction of dental clinic patients are Hepatitis B carriers?
questions.note: Part of the case for universal standard precautions and staff HBV vaccination in dental settings, regardless of a patient's known history.

questions.q: What percentage of Hepatitis C infections become chronic?
questions.ex: HCV has an unusually high chronicity rate (~85%) thanks to rapid sequence heterogeneity that lets it evade the immune response — far higher than HBV's 4-10%.

questions.q: Why can't Hepatitis D infect on its own?
questions.ans: It's a defective RNA virus that requires HBsAg (from an active Hepatitis B infection) to assemble and infect — it only occurs as an HBV co-infection or superinfection

questions.q: Hepatitis E is typically mild, except in which population, where mortality can reach 25%?
questions.ex: HEV (fecal-oral, endemic in India/Asia/Mexico) usually causes a mild 1-4 week illness, but is disproportionately severe in pregnancy.

questions.q: Approximate daily alcohol intake, sustained over 10-12 years, associated with alcoholic liver disease
questions.ans: ~80 g/day in men, ~20 g/day in women
questions.note: The lower female threshold reflects sex differences in alcohol metabolism/first-pass effect — women develop alcoholic liver disease at substantially lower cumulative doses.

questions.q: What is the correct progression of alcoholic liver disease?
ch: Steatosis (reversible) → steatohepatitis (ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies) → perivenular fibrosis → cirrhosis
questions.ex: Fat accumulation (steatosis) is reversible with abstinence; continued injury adds ballooning degeneration and Mallory-Denk bodies (steatohepatitis), then perivenular fibrosis, and finally irreversible cirrhosis.

questions.q: Which finding best fits autoimmune hepatitis rather than viral hepatitis?
ch: Female predominance (~78%), high autoantibody titers (ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM) with hypergammaglobulinemia
Elevated alkaline phosphatase out of proportion to aminotransferases
questions.ex: Autoimmune hepatitis strongly favors women, features high-titer autoantibodies and hypergammaglobulinemia, and — unlike primary biliary disease — aminotransferases rise more than alkaline phosphatase. It often responds dramatically to immunosuppression.

questions.q: Which antibiotics should be avoided entirely in patients with significant liver disease, per this lecture's dental drug list?
questions.ans: Erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline
questions.note: Contraindicated anesthetics in liver disease: halothane and thiopentone. Locals (lidocaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine) and most analgesics are liver-metabolized and need dose caution, not avoidance.

questions.q: Drug/toxin-induced hepatitis accounts for roughly what share of fulminant hepatic failure, compared to viral hepatitis?
ch: Drug-induced hepatitis never causes fulminant failure
questions.ex: Drug/toxin causes are disproportionately likely to trigger fulminant failure (10-20%) compared to viral hepatitis (~1%), even though they cause a similar share (~10%) of acute hepatitis overall.

questions.q: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency causes disease by which mechanism?
ch: Failure to secrete a misfolded protease inhibitor, which accumulates in hepatocytes while the lungs lose its protection
questions.ex: AAT is a protease inhibitor normally secreted by hepatocytes. In deficiency it isn't secreted properly, accumulating in the liver (→ cirrhosis) while its absence in the lungs leaves elastase unchecked (→ emphysema) — one autosomal recessive defect, two organs.

questions.q: Which is the correct 'most common' pairing for liver tumors?
ch: Hemangioma is the most common benign tumor; metastases are the most common liver tumor overall
Adenoma is the most common benign tumor; HCC is the most common liver tumor overall
Hemangioma is the most common benign tumor; HCC is the most common primary malignancy
questions.ex: Hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor. Among malignant tumors, metastatic disease is the most common liver tumor overall, but hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common PRIMARY liver malignancy — a classic 'most common overall vs. most common primary' distinction.

questions.q: Two conditions associated with hepatic adenoma
questions.ans: Oral contraceptive use and glycogen storage diseases

questions.q: What fraction of hepatocellular carcinomas arise in an otherwise normal (non-cirrhotic) liver?
questions.ans: Only about 10%
questions.note: The other ~90% arise on a background of chronic liver disease — alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis B/C, NAFLD, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, and glycogen storage diseases are all named risk factors.

questions.q: Match each biliary tract disorder to its location.
pairs: Adenocarcinoma, stones, inflammation of the duct itself
Stones, inflammation, tumors of the reservoir

questions.q: Per this lecture's dental/optometry clinical-relevance guidance, how long can Hepatitis C survive on surfaces — supporting standard precautions and instrument sterilization for every patient?
ch: It cannot survive outside the body
questions.ex: HCV can persist on environmental surfaces for up to 5 days, which is exactly why universal standard precautions (not just precautions for 'known' hepatitis patients) and thorough instrument sterilization matter.

questions.q: Which hepatitis virus is oral lichen planus specifically linked to, per this lecture's clinical-relevance takeaways?
questions.ans: Hepatitis C

questions.q: Per this lecture, how much more prevalent are dental erosions in GERD patients compared to those without GERD?
ch: GERD only affects the esophagus, not teeth
questions.ex: GERD patients show a 2-4x higher prevalence of dental erosion from chemical dissolution of enamel/dentin — and PPI treatment has been shown to reduce progression of that erosion, even though a direct causal relationship isn't proven.

questions.q: How might esophageal acid exposure relate to nighttime bruxism, per this lecture?
questions.ans: Esophageal acidification can induce masticatory muscle activity, and GERD patients show a higher prevalence of bruxism, especially at night; PPI treatment can reduce bruxism episodes (a direct causal link isn't proven)

questions.q: Why do NSAIDs with greater COX-1 inhibitory activity carry more GI toxicity than COX-2-selective agents?
ch: COX-1 has no role in the GI tract
COX-1 (not COX-2) produces the protective prostaglandins responsible for gastric mucus/bicarbonate output and inhibiting acid secretion
COX-2 inhibition increases acid secretion directly
questions.ex: Constitutively active COX-1 makes the prostaglandins that protect the stomach (mucus, bicarbonate, decreased acid secretion) under normal conditions; agents that hit COX-1 hard lose more of that protection than COX-2-selective drugs, which is why non-selective NSAIDs carry higher ulcer risk.

questions.q: How much does NSAID use increase the risk of peptic ulcer disease?
questions.ans: About 4-fold, with an additional increased risk of PUD complications like GI bleeding and perforation

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of US patients with peptic ulcer disease are affected by H. pylori, per this lecture?
questions.ex: H. pylori affects about 42% of US patients with PUD (though this varies by population) — it attaches to gastric mucosa and releases products that trigger inflammation, and it also raises gastric cancer risk.

questions.q: How does H2 blocker efficacy compare numerically to PPI efficacy at suppressing gastric acid secretion?
ch: H2 blockers suppress acid ~70%; PPIs suppress ~80-95% — H2 blockers are less effective but faster-onset
questions.ex: PPIs are the more powerful acid suppressors (80-95% reduction) but take 3-4 days to reach maximal effect; H2 blockers are less complete (~70% suppression) but act faster — a classic efficacy-vs-onset tradeoff.

questions.q: How can antacid-drug chelation interactions (e.g., with tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones) usually be minimized?
questions.ans: By spacing administration — taking the antacid 4 hours before or 2 hours after the interacting medication

questions.q: A patient on doxycycline for an odontogenic infection self-treats new heartburn with an OTC antacid. Which ingredient is most likely to reduce doxycycline absorption?
ch: Calcium carbonate would be the only safe option
questions.ex: Di- and trivalent cations — magnesium, aluminum, calcium — chelate tetracyclines (including doxycycline) and fluoroquinolones, reducing absorption. Sodium bicarbonate lacks this chelating cation and mainly raises gastric pH instead.

questions.q: A patient develops antibiotic-associated diarrhea and self-treats with an OTC peripheral mu-opioid receptor agonist (loperamide). What is a major mechanism by which it controls diarrhea?
ch: Decreases acetylcholine release, reducing forward peristalsis and increasing circular smooth muscle tone
questions.ex: Peripheral opioid agonists like loperamide inhibit ACh (and NO/VIP) release in the gut wall — less ACh means less longitudinal muscle contraction (less forward peristalsis) and, via less NO/VIP, more circular muscle/sphincter tone. Net effect: slower transit, more time for fluid reabsorption.

questions.q: What is the typical course and first-line management of traveler's diarrhea?
questions.ans: Usually benign and self-limited (1-5 days), over 90% bacterial (often E. coli) in most regions; first-line management is fluid replacement with electrolyte/glucose solutions, with antibiotics (often azithromycin or rifaximin) reserved for moderate-severe, bloody, or febrile cases

questions.q: Which combination of receptors is found at the area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone), a key site coordinating the vomiting reflex?
ch: 5HT3, NK1, D2, M1, CB1, and opioid receptors
questions.ex: The area postrema/CTZ integrates an unusually wide array of emetic signals — serotonin, substance P, dopamine, muscarinic, cannabinoid, and opioid receptors all converge there, part of why no single antiemetic class works for every cause of nausea.

questions.q: D2 receptor blockade outside the chemoreceptor trigger zone explains several antiemetic side effects. Which brain region/effect pairing is correct?
ch: Substantia nigra → extrapyramidal symptoms via the motor tract
questions.ex: D2 receptors in the substantia nigra regulate movement via the extrapyramidal tract — blocking them there (not just at the CTZ, where the antiemetic effect happens) produces EPS. D2 receptors in the hypothalamus (prolactin/temperature regulation) explain the hyperprolactinemia side effect.

questions.q: Typical onset timing and mortality rate of neuroleptic malignant syndrome
questions.ans: Usually occurs 1-3 days after starting the causative drug; mortality is around 10%
questions.note: Key signs: muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, mental status change, dysautonomia. Supportive care plus benzodiazepines, dantrolene, or dexmedetomidine may be used.

questions.q: Drug-induced QT prolongation is mechanistically caused by:
ch: Inhibition of the inward-rectifying potassium channel IKr, delaying repolarization
questions.ex: IKr blockade slows ventricular repolarization, prolonging the QT interval and raising the risk of torsades de pointes — a mechanism shared by droperidol, ondansetron, and dozens of other drugs, including antibiotics like levofloxacin.

questions.q: A patient on levofloxacin for an odontogenic infection receives an antiemetic before chemotherapy and develops lightheadedness with a prolonged QT on ECG. Which antiemetic is most likely responsible, compounding levofloxacin's own QT risk?
questions.ex: Ondansetron carries a recognized (if infrequent) QT-prolongation risk, and combining it with another QT-prolonging drug like levofloxacin compounds that risk — a good example of why medication reconciliation matters even for 'routine' antiemetic dosing.

questions.q: A patient needs an analgesic for pain after a dental extraction. She has a history of GERD and venous thrombosis and takes famotidine and the anticoagulant apixaban. Which analgesic choice most raises her risk of GI bleeding?
questions.ex: NSAIDs inhibit COX-1/COX-2, stripping away the protective prostaglandin tone on the gastric mucosa and raising GI bleeding risk on their own; stacked on an anticoagulant like apixaban, that risk compounds further. Acetaminophen doesn't share that mucosal-injury/antiplatelet mechanism, making it the safer analgesic choice here — a practical prescribing point for exactly the kind of patient a dentist sees after an extraction.

questions.q: All major IBD drug classes covered in this lecture are classified as DMARDs (disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs) EXCEPT:
questions.ex: Glucocorticoids are the one exception — they induce remission quickly but aren't considered disease-modifying in the same durable sense as the aminosalicylates, thiopurines, antifolates, and biologics used for maintenance.

questions.q: Methotrexate has two distinct mechanisms depending on dose. What are they?
questions.ans: At standard/higher doses: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) and thymidylate synthase, blocking purine/thymidine synthesis and therefore DNA synthesis. At the LOWER doses used for inflammatory diseases like Crohn's, the dominant mechanism is instead inhibition of AICAR transformylase, which increases adenosine — a distinct anti-inflammatory action separate from its antiproliferative effect
questions.note: A favorite exam distinction — why does low-dose MTX work for Crohn's without the full cytotoxicity of chemo doses?

questions.q: Match each feature to whether it describes Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis.
pairs: Entire GI tract (mouth to anus) can be involved

questions.q: Which oral finding is relatively specific to Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis, per this lecture?
ch: Cobblestone mucosa and orofacial granulomatosis, alongside aphthous-like ulcers and lip swelling
questions.ex: UC's oral findings are essentially limited to aphthous ulcers. Crohn's disease produces a much broader range of oral involvement — aphthous-like ulcers, mucosal swelling, cobblestone mucosa, lip swelling, and orofacial granulomatosis — reflecting its transmural, whole-GI-tract nature.

questions.q: Beyond acid-suppressing medication, what dental-specific preventive measures are recommended for GERD patients, per this lecture?
questions.ans: Fluoride supplementation, diet management, and attention to the timing of brushing (avoiding brushing immediately after a reflux/vomiting episode, when enamel is acid-softened)

questions.q: Which group of medications is specifically called out as needing metabolism-based dose caution in patients with liver disease, per this lecture?
questions.ex: Acetaminophen, opioids, sedatives, and benzodiazepines are all hepatically metabolized — in a patient with reduced hepatic reserve, standard doses can accumulate to toxic levels, making dose adjustment (and a careful running total, especially for acetaminophen) a real perioperative safety issue.

questions.q: Match each nutritional deficiency to its characteristic oral findings.
pairs: Atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, mucosal pallor

questions.q: Which specific finding explains increased bleeding risk in cirrhosis beyond just low clotting factors?
ch: Thrombocytopenia, often from splenomegaly/portal hypertension sequestering platelets
questions.ex: Cirrhosis causes bleeding risk through two separate mechanisms: reduced synthesis of clotting factors AND thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration (portal hypertension → splenomegaly). Both should be checked (PT/INR and platelet count) before invasive dental procedures.

questions.q: What is the preferred timing strategy for dental treatment in a patient who will start a bisphosphonate or denosumab?
questions.ans: Complete necessary dental treatment BEFORE starting the medication when possible, since MRONJ risk is lower before exposure begins; use atraumatic technique for any procedures needed afterward

questions.q: A patient with chronic cough, hoarseness, and dysphagia alongside dental erosion most likely has:
questions.ex: Chronic cough, hoarseness, and dysphagia are recognized extraesophageal manifestations of GERD, alongside the more familiar dental erosion and heartburn — useful for connecting a seemingly unrelated ENT complaint back to reflux.

questions.q: What is the largest and heaviest gland in the body, and roughly how much does it weigh?
questions.ans: The liver — roughly 3 pounds (about 1.4–1.6 kg)

questions.q: The liver's fibrous outer capsule is sometimes assumed to be the same tissue as the visceral peritoneum covering it. Is that correct?
ch: Yes, they are the same fibrous layer
No — the capsule (Glisson's capsule) is its own distinct fibrous layer, separate from the visceral peritoneum draped over it
No, the liver has no fibrous capsule at all
questions.ex: Glisson's capsule is the liver's own dense fibrous capsule; the visceral peritoneum is a separate serosal layer over most of it. Easy to conflate, but they're not the same tissue.

questions.q: What ligament anchors the liver to the anterior abdominal wall, and what does it split into?
questions.ans: The falciform ligament, which splits into the coronary ligaments (among others)

questions.q: Both the kidney's peritubular circulation and the liver's portal circulation route blood through two capillary beds in series before it returns to the heart. What's the key difference between them?
ch: There's no real difference — both pairs of capillary beds carry oxygenated blood throughout

In the kidney, both vessels around the first capillary bed (the glomerulus) carry oxygenated blood; in the liver, the first capillary bed sits in the GI tract itself, so blood is already deoxygenated before it ever reaches the liver's own portal-vein-to-sinusoid circulation
The kidney has three capillary beds in series, not two
The liver's first capillary bed is in the spleen, not the GI tract
questions.ex: In the nephron, the afferent and efferent arterioles around the glomerulus both carry oxygenated blood.
