In the liver's case, the 'first' capillary bed is the gut wall itself — by the time that blood collects into the portal vein it's already deoxygenated, which is exactly why the liver needs its own separate oxygenated hepatic artery supply alongside the portal vein.

questions.q: Put the venous drainage path from the hepatic lobule's central vein back to the heart in order.
steps: Central vein
Sublobular vein
Collecting vein
Hepatic vein
Inferior vena cava

questions.q: About how much bile can the gallbladder hold while storing it between meals?
questions.ans: Up to about 50 mL
questions.note: On top of storing it, the gallbladder also concentrates that bile roughly 10-fold by absorbing water and electrolytes.

questions.q: What's a simple bedside trick for getting a clearer ultrasound view of the liver, and why does it work?
questions.ans: Have the patient take a deep breath — the diaphragm pushes the liver down from under the costal margin into better view
questions.note: Most of the liver normally sits tucked up under the rib cage, so this is a quick way to bring more of it into the ultrasound window.

questions.q: What landmark marks the transition from the duodenum to the jejunum?
questions.ans: The ligament of Treitz
questions.note: It's also the classic radiographic/surgical landmark separating 'upper' from 'lower' GI bleeding.

questions.q: What structurally distinguishes a plica (circularis) from a villus?
ch: A plica contains a submucosal core; a villus does not — it's built from mucosal epithelium and lamina propria alone
A villus contains a submucosal core; a plica does not
Neither structure contains any connective tissue
questions.ex: A plica is a larger permanent fold that pulls the submucosa along with it — vessels and connective tissue are visible inside one on a slide. A villus is a smaller finger-like projection of just the mucosa (epithelium plus lamina propria) with no submucosal core of its own; villi actually line the surface of plicae.

questions.q: How does villus prominence change moving from the duodenum toward the colon?
ch: Villi stay exactly the same size and number throughout the entire GI tract
Villi gradually get smaller and less numerous from the duodenum through the ileum, then disappear completely in the colon
Villi are absent in the small intestine and only appear in the colon
Villi abruptly disappear right at the duodenojejunal junction
questions.ex: It's a gradient, not a cliff — villi are tallest and most numerous proximally and progressively taper off through the jejunum and ileum, then vanish entirely in the colon, which relies on crypts alone.

questions.q: What three vascular/lymphatic structures run through the core of a single intestinal villus?
questions.ans: A small artery, a vein, and a surrounding capillary network — plus a central lacteal (lymphatic capillary)
questions.note: The lacteal is what carries chylomicrons away from the enterocyte into the lymphatic system.

questions.q: Villi contain a thin strand of smooth muscle in their core, distinct from the contractile microfilaments inside each microvillus. What does this smooth muscle do?
ch: Lets the whole villus sway/contract slightly, likely under enteric nervous system control, helping move luminal contents
questions.ex: Two separate contractile systems, two scales: microfilaments inside each microvillus let the brush border itself move at the subcellular level, while a separate strand of smooth muscle running up into the villus core lets the entire villus sway — both aimed at keeping luminal contents moving across the absorptive surface.

questions.q: Inside the enterocyte, absorbed fatty acids/monoglycerides are re-esterified into triglycerides and packaged with apolipoproteins into chylomicrons. Which organelles handle each half of that job?
ch: Smooth ER resynthesizes the triglyceride core; rough ER synthesizes the apolipoprotein coat
Rough ER resynthesizes the triglyceride core; smooth ER synthesizes the apolipoprotein coat
The Golgi apparatus does both jobs alone
Mitochondria resynthesize the triglycerides; the nucleus makes the apolipoproteins
questions.ex: Smooth ER (no ribosomes) is the lipid-handling organelle, so it re-esterifies fatty acids/monoglycerides into triglycerides; rough ER (ribosome-studded) does the protein synthesis, making the apolipoprotein coat — together they hand off a finished chylomicron for exocytosis toward the lacteal.

questions.q: Describe the characteristic shape and internal organization of a goblet cell.
questions.ans: Mucinogen granules pack the apical cytoplasm, pushing the nucleus toward the base — giving the cell a 'V' or goblet shape
questions.note: Goblet cells increase in number from the duodenum toward the ileum, and increase further still in the colon.

questions.q: Match each GI hormone to its main action.
pairs: Stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric epithelial proliferation
Gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion
Increases motility in the stomach and small intestine
Inhibits gastrin secretion and gastric motility

questions.q: What's the key difference between the internal and external anal sphincter?
ch: Both are smooth muscle, under involuntary control only
The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle (involuntary); the external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle (voluntary)
The internal sphincter is skeletal muscle (voluntary); the external is smooth muscle (involuntary)
Both are skeletal muscle, under voluntary control only
questions.ex: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the muscularis externa's circular smooth muscle — involuntary. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, which is exactly what allows conscious deferral of defecation.

questions.q: Which substance can both damage the gastric mucosal barrier and stimulate gastric acid secretion, making it a forerunner of gastric ulcer?
questions.ex: H. pylori's urease converts urea to ammonia, which is protonated to ammonium in the acidic stomach; the ammonium both damages the mucosal barrier and increases parietal cell mass/acid output — a double hit that promotes ulcer formation. Bile salts can damage the barrier but don't meaningfully affect acid secretion; EGF and mucus strengthen the barrier.

questions.q: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is caused by a mutation in which gene?
questions.ans: APC (adenomatous polyposis coli)
questions.note: Autosomal dominant, essentially 100% lifetime risk of malignant transformation — which is why FAP is managed with prophylactic colectomy rather than surveillance alone.

questions.q: Esophageal carcinoma strongly associated with alcohol and tobacco use is:
questions.ex: Squamous cell carcinoma tracks tobacco, alcohol, and nitrosamine exposure. Its US incidence has been declining as adenocarcinoma (tied instead to Barrett esophagus and reflux) has become more common — now over half of US esophageal cancer.

questions.q: Roughly what share of US cancer deaths does colorectal adenocarcinoma account for, and how does it rank?
ch: About 9% of US cancer deaths — the 2nd most common cause
About 25% of US cancer deaths — the most common cause
About 2% of US cancer deaths — a rare cause
About 9% of US cancer deaths, but only in men
questions.ex: The lecture's own slide states colorectal adenocarcinoma is the 2nd most common cause of US cancer deaths at about 9%. (One of the course's practice-question sources instead labels it '3rd most common' — a figure that may be conflating cause-of-death ranking with incidence ranking, since colorectal cancer is also commonly cited as the 3rd most commonly diagnosed cancer. Worth confirming which figure the exam wants.)

questions.q: Define a hiatal hernia.
questions.ans: Herniation of the stomach through an enlarged esophageal hiatus in the diaphragm
questions.note: A sliding hiatal hernia is one of the mechanisms behind a weak LES and reflux esophagitis.

questions.q: Esophageal varices are:
ch: Dilated submucosal veins in the distal esophagus from portal hypertension, asymptomatic until rupture
Dilated mucosal arteries in the proximal esophagus from systemic hypertension
A benign tumor of esophageal smooth muscle
questions.ex: Varices form when portal hypertension (usually from hepatic cirrhosis) forces blood through submucosal esophageal veins that were never built for the pressure. They're silent until they rupture — and rupture is fatal roughly 40% of the time.

questions.q: Which histologic features point to reflux esophagitis rather than a normal esophageal mucosa?
ch: Hyperemia, basal zone hyperplasia, increased intraepithelial eosinophils/neutrophils, and elongated lamina propria papillae
Prominent eosinophilic microabscesses at a normal luminal pH
questions.ex: Those four features (hyperemia, basal hyperplasia, mixed intraepithelial inflammation, elongated papillae) are the classic reflux pattern. Eosinophilic microabscesses at normal pH describe eosinophilic esophagitis instead; flattened villi describe celiac disease; granulomas describe Crohn disease.

questions.q: A patient fails anti-reflux therapy, has episodes of food impaction, and biopsy shows prominent intraepithelial eosinophilia with microabscesses at a normal esophageal pH. This is:
questions.ex: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a distinct clinicopathologic entity from GERD — normal pH, anti-reflux-drug failure, food impaction, and a dense eosinophilic infiltrate with microabscesses are what separate it from reflux esophagitis.

questions.q: Name the three infectious causes of esophagitis covered in this lecture.
questions.ans: Candida, herpes simplex virus, and cytomegalovirus
questions.note: Chemical esophagitis (from caustic ingestion — acids, alkalis, hot liquids, smoke — or radiotherapy) is the other major non-reflux category.

questions.q: Barrett esophagus is best defined as:
ch: Intestinal metaplasia (with goblet cells) replacing squamous epithelium above the gastroesophageal junction
Squamous metaplasia of the gastric cardia
A benign submucosal leiomyoma of the distal esophagus
Dilated submucosal veins from portal hypertension
questions.ex: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia — recognizable by goblet cells — appearing as velvety, salmon-colored mucosa above the GE junction in chronic reflux patients (present in roughly 5-15% of those with chronic reflux esophagitis, more common in white males). It raises adenocarcinoma risk 30-100 fold.

questions.q: When a biopsy is signed out as Barrett esophagus, what must the pathology report explicitly address, and why?
questions.ans: The presence or absence of dysplasia — because dysplasia is what typically precedes progression to adenocarcinoma
questions.note: This is a direct, explicitly emphasized reporting requirement from the lecture, not just background detail.

questions.q: Which statement about esophageal cancer epidemiology in the US is correct?
ch: Adenocarcinoma, tied to Barrett esophagus, now makes up over 50% of esophageal cancer and continues to rise while SCC declines
SCC has always been rare and adenocarcinoma has always dominated
Both SCC and adenocarcinoma have declined equally over the past 50 years
Adenocarcinoma is declining as SCC becomes more common
questions.ex: The pattern has flipped: SCC (tobacco/alcohol/nitrosamine-driven) used to dominate but is declining, while adenocarcinoma (Barrett/reflux-driven) is now over half of US esophageal cancer and still rising.

questions.q: Match each gastritis subtype to its typical cause.
pairs: Direct mucosal irritation by iron supplements
Autoimmune destruction of parietal cell mass

questions.q: Why does atrophic (autoimmune) gastritis cause vitamin B12 deficiency?
ch: It destroys the parietal cells that make intrinsic factor, which B12 needs for ileal absorption
It destroys chief cells, which make pepsinogen needed to digest B12-containing proteins
It causes malabsorption by flattening small-intestinal villi
It directly binds and inactivates circulating B12
questions.ex: Parietal cells make both HCl and intrinsic factor. Autoimmune/atrophic gastritis destroys the parietal cell mass, so intrinsic factor production falls — and without intrinsic factor, the terminal ileum can't absorb B12, regardless of dietary intake.

questions.q: Which benign gastric lesion nonetheless carries real malignant potential, unlike the other mesenchymal lesions it's grouped with?
questions.ex: GIST arises from the stomach's own benign pacemaker cells (interstitial cells of Cajal) but, unlike a simple leiomyoma or lipoma, carries genuine malignant potential and needs to be followed/managed accordingly.

questions.q: Fundic gland polyps are associated with which two settings?
questions.ans: Sporadic occurrence (the more common pattern) and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
questions.note: Some evidence also links sporadic fundic gland polyps to long-term proton pump inhibitor use.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognized risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma?
ch: A diet high in cured, smoked, or pickled foods
questions.ex: Gastric adenocarcinoma risk tracks H. pylori infection, atrophic gastritis, smoking, and diets heavy in cured/smoked/pickled foods — not a high-fiber, low-fat diet, which is protective rather than causative for most GI cancers discussed in this block.

questions.q: Match each gross growth pattern of gastric carcinoma to its description.
pairs: Fungating mass projecting into the lumen
Erosive, may mimic a benign peptic ulcer
Diffusely thickens and stiffens the wall — 'leather bottle stomach'
Minimal elevation or depression, subtle on endoscopy

questions.q: A gastric adenocarcinoma with cells whose nuclei are pushed to the periphery by intracytoplasmic mucin is:
questions.ex: Signet ring cells — mucin-filled cytoplasm displacing the nucleus to one side — are the hallmark of diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma, distinct from the gland-forming intestinal type.

questions.q: What is the most common type of gastric lymphoma, and what is it associated with?
questions.ans: MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphoma, associated with H. pylori infection
questions.note: This is one reason H. pylori eradication is sometimes curative for early gastric MALT lymphoma.

questions.q: A duodenal biopsy shows flattened villi and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. A second biopsy shows increased intraepithelial lymphocytes with normal villous architecture. These findings represent, respectively:
ch: Active celiac disease, then 'latent' celiac disease
questions.ex: Celiac disease classically flattens villi while packing the epithelium with lymphocytes; a 'latent' pattern shows the lymphocytic infiltrate present while villous architecture is still preserved — an earlier or milder point on the same disease spectrum.

questions.q: What is the typical pathogenesis of acute appendicitis?
ch: Obstruction of the appendiceal orifice (fecalith, tumor, parasite, or no identifiable cause) causing luminal distention and bacterial invasion
An autoimmune reaction against the appendiceal mucosa
Viral infection alone, without bacterial involvement
questions.ex: Obstruction — most often a fecalith, sometimes a tumor, parasite, or foreign body, and in many cases no obstruction is ever identified — leads to distention and secondary bacterial invasion, producing the fibrinopurulent exudate, microabscesses, and transmural inflammation seen on pathology, with perforation as the major risk.

questions.q: Where is the classic 'watershed area' most vulnerable to ischemic colitis, and why?
questions.ans: The splenic flexure — it sits at the boundary between two separate arterial supplies (SMA and IMA territory), so it's the last area reached by either and the first to suffer when perfusion drops
questions.note: Histologic changes include surface mucin loss, lamina propria hyalinization, and crypt withering/dropout.

questions.q: What's the relationship between diverticular disease and diverticulitis?
ch: They're the same thing, just different names

Diverticular disease is the (usually asymptomatic) presence of diverticula from muscle weakness and a low-fiber diet; diverticulitis is perforation/inflammation of one, which can cause LLQ pain, fever, bleeding, or abscess
Diverticular disease only occurs in the small intestine
questions.ex: Most diverticular disease is silent. Diverticulitis is the complication — inflammation or micro-perforation of a diverticulum — that actually produces symptoms.

questions.q: A patient has severe watery diarrhea, but colonoscopy shows a completely normal-appearing colon. What's the most likely diagnosis, and how is it confirmed?
ch: Microscopic colitis, confirmed only by biopsy
Ulcerative colitis, confirmed by the gross appearance alone
questions.ex: Microscopic colitis (lymphocytic or collagenous subtype) is, by definition, invisible on gross colonoscopic exam — the colitis is only apparent on histology, which is why biopsy is required even when the colon 'looks fine.'

questions.q: Match each pathologic feature to whether it's characteristic of Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis.
pairs: Skip lesions with intervening normal mucosa
Continuous involvement starting at the rectum

questions.q: Put the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in the correct order.
steps: Normal mucosal surface and crypt epithelium
Aberrant crypt foci
Adenomatous polyp (usually tubular adenoma)
Invasive carcinoma
Metastatic carcinoma

questions.q: A colorectal tumor on the left (descending colon) versus one on the right (ascending colon) tend to present differently. Why?
ch: Left-sided tumors cause early obstruction (cramping, altered bowel habits) because the lumen is narrower and stool is more formed there; right-sided tumors more often present silently with iron deficiency anemia from occult bleeding into a wider, more liquid-content lumen
Right-sided tumors always obstruct first; left-sided tumors are always silent
Location has no effect on presentation
Left-sided tumors only cause anemia; right-sided tumors only cause obstruction
questions.ex: The descending colon has a narrower lumen and firmer stool, so a tumor there tends to obstruct and change bowel habits early. The ascending colon is wider with liquid contents, so a tumor there can bleed slowly and silently for a long time, surfacing only as iron deficiency anemia.

questions.q: Match each GI symptom term to its meaning.
pairs: Passing dark, tarry blood in the stool

questions.q: What distinguishes a paraesophageal hiatal hernia from a sliding hiatal hernia?
ch: In a paraesophageal hernia the gastroesophageal junction stays in its normal position while part of the gastric fundus herniates alongside it through the hiatus; in a sliding hernia the junction itself moves up and down across the diaphragm
A paraesophageal hernia only occurs in the distal colon
A sliding hernia is always more dangerous and requires emergency surgery
There is no meaningful anatomic difference between the two
questions.ex: In a sliding hiatal hernia, the GE junction itself slides above and below the diaphragm. In a paraesophageal hernia, the junction stays anchored in its normal position but a portion of the fundus herniates up beside it — a distinct anatomic variant, not just a matter of degree.

questions.q: What gene mutation drives most GISTs, and why did this matter historically for cancer therapy?
questions.ans: A mutation in KIT (CKIT); GIST was one of the first tumor types treatable with a targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor
questions.note: This molecular-targeted-therapy history is part of why GIST gets tested disproportionately often relative to how common it actually is in practice.

questions.q: Why does the stomach have two histologically distinct types of mucosa in different regions?
ch: The fundus/body carry acid-producing (oxyntic) mucosa with parietal and chief cells, while the cardia and antrum carry protective, mucus-secreting mucosa that buffers acid at both the esophageal and duodenal ends
All regions of the stomach have identical mucosa and cell populations
Only the antrum makes acid; the fundus and body are purely mucus-secreting
The cardia makes acid to kill ingested pathogens before they reach the body of the stomach
questions.ex: Oxyntic (acid/pepsinogen-producing) mucosa dominates the fundus and body. The cardia and antrum instead carry more protective mucus-secreting glands — buffering reflux at the GE junction and buffering what empties into the duodenum, respectively.

questions.q: Which part of the GI tract does Crohn disease characteristically favor, even though it can involve any segment from mouth to anus?
questions.ans: The terminal ileum and right colon
questions.note: Aphthous oral ulcers are also a common Crohn's finding and can be a patient's presenting complaint.

questions.q: Why does Crohn disease, more than ulcerative colitis, lead to fistulas, adhesions, and bowel obstruction?
ch: Because its inflammation is transmural (full bowel-wall thickness), so scarring and abnormal tissue connections can form between the bowel and adjacent structures
Because Crohn disease only affects the mucosa, making the wall structurally weaker
Because ulcerative colitis is a more severe disease overall
Fistulas and obstruction are equally common in both diseases for the same reason
questions.ex: Because Crohn's fissuring ulcers cut through the full thickness of the bowel wall, chronic inflammation there can scar into adhesions, tunnel into fistulas (bowel-to-bowel, bowel-to-bladder, etc.), and narrow the lumen into obstruction — complications that track directly with how deep the inflammation goes, not just how severe the diarrhea is.

questions.q: Name three extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease outside the GI tract.
questions.ans: Uveitis (eyes), arthritis (joints), and sclerosing cholangitis (bile ducts/liver) — kidney involvement can also occur
questions.note: Both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis can produce these; a patient presenting with unexplained uveitis or arthritis is worth asking about bowel symptoms.

questions.q: Besides FAP, what is the other major hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome, and what does it also raise risk for?
questions.ans: HNPCC (hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer), also called Lynch syndrome — it also raises risk for several other cancer types beyond the colon
questions.note: Unlike FAP, HNPCC/Lynch syndrome does not cause innumerable colon polyps — a distinct genetic mechanism, which is why family history matters even without a polyposis picture.

questions.q: What change in average-risk colorectal cancer screening has occurred in recent years, and why?
ch: The recommended starting age for screening colonoscopy was lowered from 50 to 45, because colon cancer incidence has been rising sharply in patients under 50 even as it declines in older adults
The recommended starting age was raised from 45 to 50, because colon cancer has become vanishingly rare in younger adults
Screening recommendations have not changed in decades
Colonoscopy is no longer the recommended screening method for anyone
questions.ex: Colon cancer death rates have been falling in the traditionally 'older' population, but incidence has been climbing steadily in patients under 50 — enough that the average-risk starting age for screening moved from 50 down to 45.

questions.q: What is a 'napkin ring' lesion in colorectal cancer, and what symptom does it commonly cause?
questions.ans: A colorectal carcinoma that grows circumferentially all the way around the bowel wall — often ulcerated and bleeding, and prone to causing obstruction
questions.note: The circumferential growth narrows the lumen the way a napkin ring narrows around a napkin — a visual pattern distinct from an exophytic mass.

questions.q: Has US gastric (stomach) adenocarcinoma incidence been rising or falling over recent decades, and what's the leading theory why?
questions.ans: Falling — thought to reflect better food preservation reducing exposure to bacterial and other contaminants historically linked to stomach cancer risk
questions.note: Contrast with colorectal cancer, whose incidence is rising in patients under 50 — the two GI cancers are trending in opposite directions.

questions.q: A patient has iron deficiency anemia with no obvious dietary or gynecologic explanation. What should this prompt?
ch: A workup to rule out chronic GI blood loss, including malignancy, since unexplained anemia is a red flag for a GI source
Reassurance, since anemia without bleeding symptoms is rarely GI-related
Immediate colonoscopic decompression, without further workup
A repeat CBC in one year
questions.ex: Slow, chronic GI blood loss — from a tumor, bleeding ulcer, or precancerous polyp — can present as nothing but anemia. Unexplained anemia should prompt a GI workup to rule out malignancy or another bleeding source, not be dismissed.

questions.q: Match each surgical bowel-obstruction term to its definition.
pairs: Bowel or intestinal contents protruding somewhere they shouldn't (inguinal, umbilical, incisional, or hiatal) — risks strangulation if the trapped segment's blood supply is cut off
Scar tissue, usually from prior surgery or inflammation, binding loops of bowel together and causing obstruction or twisting
The bowel twisting on itself and compromising its own blood supply — most classically the sigmoid colon, sometimes reducible endoscopically
One segment of bowel telescoping into an adjacent segment, often around a lead point like a lymph node or small tumor

questions.q: Besides the splenic-flexure watershed anatomy, what patient risk factors predispose to ischemic bowel disease?
questions.ans: Advanced age, hypertension, diabetes, prior abdominal surgery, and certain medications or infections
questions.note: These are the same vascular risk factors you'd associate with atherosclerotic disease elsewhere in the body — ischemic bowel disease is, at its core, a vascular problem.

questions.q: Roughly how much fluid is presented to the small intestine each day, and how much of it is normally reabsorbed?
questions.ans: About 9 L total (roughly 2 L from oral intake plus about 7 L of endogenous GI secretions) — the small and large intestine together reabsorb about 99% of it, leaving well under 200 mL to leave in the stool
questions.note: This is the volume context that makes both vomiting and diarrhea dangerous — even a modest percentage drop in reabsorption efficiency represents a large absolute fluid loss.

questions.q: Functionally, how do the villus and the crypt divide labor in the small intestine?
ch: The villus, built from differentiated absorptive enterocytes, does most of the absorbing; the crypt, built from undifferentiated cells, does most of the secreting
The crypt does the absorbing and the villus does the secreting
Both structures absorb and secrete equally, with no functional division
Only the crypt participates in fluid transport — the villus is exclusively for nutrient absorption, not fluid
questions.ex: Absorption and secretion are spatially separated: villus enterocytes (differentiated, absorptive) pull fluid and solute out of the lumen, while crypt cells (undifferentiated, more stem-like) drive secretion into it — the two together set the net fluid balance.

questions.q: Are villus (absorptive) and crypt (secretory) cells permanently separate populations? Describe what actually happens over a cell's life cycle.
questions.ans: No — crypt cells continuously migrate up toward the villus tip, undergoing a real shift in gene expression from a secretory to an absorptive program as they climb, before finally being sloughed off at the villus tip
questions.note: The same cell lineage changes jobs as it migrates; it isn't that two fixed cell populations exist side by side.

questions.q: Match each intercellular junction type to its main role in the gut epithelium.
pairs: Seals the paracellular space at the apical edge — the primary determinant of how 'leaky' or 'tight' the epithelium is
Anchors the actin cytoskeleton, with comparatively little structural strength
Anchors intermediate filaments — the real structural support keeping a cell upright
Allows direct cell-to-cell passage of ions, small molecules, and signals
Anchors the basolateral surface to the basement membrane, preventing premature sloughing

questions.q: Junction 'tightness' is measured as transepithelial resistance (Rte). Which of these is the extreme high-Rte example used to illustrate just how tight an epithelial barrier can get?
ch: The gallbladder, at a very low Rte
Frog skin, at a very high Rte (up to roughly 90 mV)
The small intestine, at a moderate Rte
Cardiac muscle, which has no measurable Rte
questions.ex: Frog skin is cited as an extreme example of a tight barrier (high Rte, up to ~90 mV) — a frog needs real protection from its unclean pond environment. The gallbladder sits at the opposite end, deliberately leaky so it can lose water readily to concentrate bile.

questions.q: Within the gut itself, how does colon junction tightness compare to the small intestine's, and why does that make physiological sense?
questions.ans: The colon's junctions are tighter (higher Rte) than the small intestine's, consistent with the colon's job of containing its dense resident bacterial population — something the small intestine doesn't have to the same degree
questions.note: Tightness tracks the job: more bacteria to contain, tighter the seal needs to be.

questions.q: Once SGLT1 has concentrated glucose inside the enterocyte, how does that glucose then cross the basolateral membrane into blood?
ch: GLUT2, via facilitated diffusion — no additional coupling needed, since the concentration gradient already favors glucose leaving the cell
A second sodium-coupled transporter identical to SGLT1
It cannot cross the basolateral membrane and is stored as glycogen in the enterocyte instead
questions.ex: SGLT1 does the uphill work apically, using the sodium gradient to concentrate glucose inside the cell against its own gradient. Once that gradient favors efflux, GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane just lets glucose diffuse out into blood — simple facilitated diffusion, no coupling required.

questions.q: How are the apical Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) and the apical Cl-/HCO3- exchanger functionally linked in the second absorptive mechanism?
ch: They are unrelated — NHE3 works in the small intestine, the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger works only in the colon

NHE3 brings sodium in while pumping a proton out, which would acidify the lumen; the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger neutralizes that by sending bicarbonate out and bringing chloride in — net result, both sodium and chloride are absorbed
The Cl-/HCO3- exchanger powers NHE3 directly via a shared ATPase
NHE3 only functions after the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger has finished its cycle
questions.ex: The two exchangers are coupled to keep the lumen from acidifying: NHE3's proton output would drop luminal pH, so the paired Cl-/HCO3- exchanger sends bicarbonate back out to neutralize it while pulling chloride in. Net effect: sodium and chloride both enter the cell, sodium exits basolaterally via the Na+/K+-ATPase, and water follows osmotically. Unlike SGLT1, this mechanism operates in both the small intestine and the colon.

questions.q: Where is ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) active, and what does it do?
questions.ans: ENaC is restricted to the colon, where it simply lets sodium enter the apical membrane on its own — paired with a separate potassium channel that keeps potassium cycling rather than accumulating
questions.note: Unlike the other two absorptive mechanisms, ENaC needs no coupled ion exchange — it's a simple channel, not a transporter.

questions.q: Match each absorptive mechanism to where along the gut it operates.
pairs: Sodium-coupled glucose transport (SGLT1 apical / GLUT2 basolateral)
Both the small intestine and the colon
Water absorption that follows all three mechanisms
Passive, driven by the osmotic gradient the solute absorption creates — no dedicated water transporter

questions.q: How does NKCC1 set up crypt-cell secretion before the cell is ever stimulated?
ch: It sits open at the apical membrane, continuously leaking chloride into the lumen

It's a basolateral Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter that uses the inward sodium gradient (maintained by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase) to drag chloride into the cell against its own gradient, building up a large intracellular chloride pool ready for release
It actively pumps chloride out of the cell using ATP
It only becomes active after CFTR has already opened
questions.ex: NKCC1 is a basolateral loading step, not the release step — it piggybacks on the sodium gradient to build up intracellular chloride at rest. The apical CFTR channel is what actually releases that stored chloride into the lumen once the cell is stimulated.

questions.q: When a crypt cell is stimulated (e.g., by a meal), what happens, and why does this same channel matter in cystic fibrosis?
questions.ans: The apical CFTR channel opens and releases the chloride NKCC1 has stockpiled into the lumen, with sodium and water following — CFTR is the same channel defective in cystic fibrosis, which is why CF causes thick secretions in organs (like the lung) that depend on CFTR-driven chloride and fluid movement

questions.q: Put the steps of the vomiting reflex in the correct order.
steps: Hypersalivation (protects the teeth and oral cavity from acidic vomitus)
Reverse peristalsis moves upper-small-intestinal contents back into the stomach
The glottis closes to prevent aspiration
Abdominal wall muscles contract, raising intra-abdominal pressure
The lower esophageal sphincter and esophagus relax
Forceful ejection of gastric contents

questions.q: Match each vomiting trigger to the medullary region that responds to it.
pairs: Circulating toxins or drugs, sampled directly from blood or CSF
Chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema) — unprotected by the blood-brain barrier
Fear, anticipation, intense pain, or strong smells
Motion and vertigo, relayed through the labyrinth and cerebellum

questions.q: Why does severe nausea often require more than one antiemetic drug class at once?
ch: All antiemetics work through the exact same receptor, so combining them is just redundant reinforcement

The three vomiting-triggering pathways converge on a shared final output but aren't identical, so a single drug class targeting only one pathway (e.g., an antihistamine/anticholinergic at the chemoreceptor trigger zone and vestibular pathway) can miss triggers acting through another (e.g., a 5-HT3 antagonist's target at the level of the nucleus tractus solitarius)
Antiemetics lose potency after a single dose regardless of cause
Only the vomiting center itself can be pharmacologically targeted
questions.ex: Because the chemoreceptor trigger zone, nucleus tractus solitarius, and vomiting center each respond to different triggers and are targeted by different drug classes, a nausea source that recruits more than one pathway often needs more than one class covered at once — this is exactly why antiemetics are usually chosen by which pathway they target.

questions.q: What acid-base disturbance does vomiting cause, and what's the body's first response?
ch: Metabolic alkalosis, compensated by reduced ventilation (retaining CO2)
Respiratory alkalosis, with no metabolic compensation
No acid-base disturbance — only electrolyte changes
questions.ex: Vomiting empties acidic gastric contents, producing a metabolic alkalosis. The first compensatory response is respiratory: reduced ventilation retains CO2 to push the pH back toward normal.

questions.q: Vomiting causes hypokalemia through two separate mechanisms. Name both.
questions.ans: (1) Intracellular hydrogen shifts out of cells in exchange for potassium moving in, lowering extracellular/plasma potassium, and (2) extracellular volume contraction stimulates aldosterone, which drives further renal potassium wasting
questions.note: Two independent mechanisms pushing the same direction — worth knowing both rather than just 'vomiting causes low potassium.'

questions.q: Match each diarrhea category to its underlying mechanism.
pairs: Unabsorbed solute (from lactose intolerance, celiac disease, or a villus-flattening infection) holds water in the lumen osmotically while crypt secretion continues unopposed
Excessive peristalsis or reduced segmentation allows bacterial overgrowth that ferments carbohydrate into gas, and fluid isn't reclaimed by the time it reaches the colon
Direct overactivation of CFTR-mediated chloride secretion — from agents like VIP, irritant laxatives, certain metals, plant toxins, or bacterial toxins such as cholera
A breakdown of the epithelial barrier itself, as in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis

questions.q: What is the mechanism behind cholera's profuse watery diarrhea?
ch: Direct mechanical damage to the villus tips by the bacteria

The toxin's B subunit binds the GM1 ganglioside receptor, letting the A subunit lock the Gs-alpha subunit permanently 'on,' which drives adenylate cyclase to massively overproduce cAMP — and that cAMP phosphorylates and opens CFTR
Cholera toxin directly blocks NHE3 with no second-messenger involvement
Cholera works by destroying the tight junctions between enterocytes
questions.ex: Cholera hijacks the same CFTR-mediated secretory pathway crypt cells use physiologically, but locks it permanently open via a cAMP flood — producing liters-per-day fluid loss that kills primarily through dehydration, not the toxin's direct tissue effect.

questions.q: Traveler's diarrhea's heat-stable toxin reaches the same CFTR channel cholera does, but by a different route. How?
ch: It also raises cAMP via the identical Gs-alpha mechanism as cholera
It inhibits NHE3 (blocking sodium/proton exchange) and raises cyclic GMP, which also stimulates CFTR
It works entirely independently of CFTR
It lowers intracellular calcium to open CFTR
questions.ex: Different second messenger, same destination: cholera drives cAMP through a locked-on Gs-alpha, while the traveler's-diarrhea heat-stable toxin instead inhibits NHE3 and raises cGMP — both pathways converge on opening CFTR.

questions.q: What acid-base disturbance does diarrhea cause, and how does the body compensate?
questions.ans: Metabolic acidosis, because diarrhea empties bicarbonate-rich fluid from below the pylorus — the mirror image of vomiting's alkalosis — compensated by hyperventilation
questions.note: Where the fluid is lost from (above vs. below the pylorus) predicts the direction of the acid-base disturbance.

questions.q: Diarrhea also causes hypokalemia, but through a different route than vomiting does. What's the mechanism?
questions.ans: Aldosterone-driven renal potassium loss — as the kidney works to reclaim sodium and volume lost in the stool, it wastes potassium as a side effect
questions.note: Contrast with vomiting's hypokalemia, which comes from two separate mechanisms (an intracellular H+/K+ shift plus aldosterone) — diarrhea's is aldosterone-driven alone.

questions.q: Match each agent to how it modulates intestinal fluid transport.
pairs: Promotes sodium (and water) absorption, especially in the colon
Promotes secretion via the cAMP/CFTR pathway — the same pathway a VIPoma pathologically overactivates

questions.q: Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis while diarrhea causes metabolic acidosis — opposite directions. Why?
ch: Because vomiting and diarrhea use entirely different electrolytes

Because the fluid lost in each case differs in exactly where along the GI tract it comes from: vomiting empties acidic contents from above the pylorus, while diarrhea empties bicarbonate-rich fluid from below it
Because only diarrhea involves the kidney
Because vomiting never affects blood pH, only diarrhea does
questions.ex: Acid-base direction tracks anatomic source: gastric contents (above the pylorus) are acidic, so losing them alkalinizes the blood; bicarbonate-rich intestinal/pancreaticobiliary secretions (below the pylorus) are what diarrhea loses, so losing them acidifies the blood.

questions.q: A patient with untreated celiac disease has chronic watery diarrhea that improves substantially with fasting. A different patient with small bowel bacterial overgrowth has diarrhea plus excess gas that does NOT resolve as cleanly with fasting. What distinguishes their mechanisms?
ch: The celiac patient's diarrhea is malabsorptive/osmotic — unabsorbed solute (from a damaged villus) holds water in the lumen only as long as that solute keeps arriving, so it improves with fasting; the overgrowth patient's diarrhea is driven by excessive motility letting bacteria ferment carbohydrate into gas, a mechanism fasting alone doesn't fully correct
Both are inflammatory diarrhea from epithelial barrier breakdown
Neither has anything to do with the small intestine
questions.ex: Osmotic diarrhea classically improves with fasting because it depends on continued delivery of unabsorbed solute; motility-driven diarrhea with bacterial overgrowth doesn't resolve the same way, since the underlying problem is transit/mixing dynamics and bacterial fermentation rather than solute load alone — a useful bedside distinction between two of the four diarrhea categories.

questions.q: Glycogen synthesis has a zonal quirk depending on the substrate used. What is it?
ch: Synthesis from both lactate and glucose is highest in Zone 1 and lowest in Zone 3

Synthesis from lactate runs highest in Zone 1 and lowest in Zone 3, while synthesis from glucose runs the opposite way — highest in Zone 3, lowest in Zone 1 — so despite this zone-specific wiring, glycogen ends up visible throughout the lobule rather than concentrated in one zone
Glycogen synthesis only occurs in Zone 3, regardless of substrate
Zone 1 and Zone 3 are equally incapable of glycogen synthesis
questions.ex: The two substrates are wired in opposite zonal directions, which sounds like it should produce a zone-specific glycogen pattern — but the net effect is the opposite: glycogen ends up distributed throughout the lobule because each zone is compensating for the other's substrate preference.

questions.q: Mechanistically, why does lactulose treat hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.ans: Gut bacteria fermenting the non-absorbable sugar lactulose generate short-chain fatty acids that protonate ammonia (NH3) to ammonium (NH4+) right in the colon, trapping it there for fecal excretion instead of letting it diffuse into portal blood in the first place
questions.note: This works because of a solubility difference: NH3 is lipid-soluble and crosses membranes freely, while charged NH4+ cannot.

questions.q: What property of ammonia (NH3) versus ammonium (NH4+) makes lactulose's trapping strategy work?
ch: NH3 is lipid-soluble and diffuses freely across membranes; its charged form NH4+ does not
NH4+ is lipid-soluble and NH3 is not
Both forms cross membranes equally well
Neither form can cross any biological membrane
questions.ex: NH3, being uncharged, slips across lipid membranes freely — which is exactly the problem in liver failure, since it can diffuse from gut to portal blood to systemic circulation to the brain. Protonating it to NH4+ in the colon (lactulose's mechanism) traps it there because the charged form can't follow that same path.

questions.q: Put the lipoprotein cascade in order, from a chylomicron leaving the gut to its clearance from blood.
steps: A chylomicron, assembled in the gut, enters systemic circulation
Lipoprotein lipase at capillary walls strips out free fatty acids and glycerol
The remaining remnant chylomicron returns to the liver
The liver repackages it with fresh triglyceride and cholesterol as VLDL and releases it
Lipoprotein lipase shrinks VLDL further into IDL, then LDL, as it hands off its cargo
The LDL receptor clears the particle from blood

questions.q: How does HDL's job differ from the VLDL-to-LDL cascade, and what receptor does it use?
questions.ans: HDL runs the opposite direction — made by both gut and liver, it scavenges cholesterol out of peripheral cell membranes and returns it to the liver's own pool via the SR-B1 receptor
questions.note: VLDL/IDL/LDL deliver lipid outward to tissues; HDL is the return trip, bringing cholesterol back to the liver.

questions.q: Match each drug/hormone biotransformation step to where it's zonally concentrated in the liver.
pairs: Most Phase I CYP450 oxidation and glucuronide conjugation
Zone 1 — where there's little CYP450 to feed a Phase I intermediate into glucuronidation
Ethanol oxidation above ~100 mg/dL (the CYP2E1-based backup pathway)
Zone 3 — the same zone (and often the same enzyme machinery) handling ordinary drug detoxification

questions.q: Why is heavy alcohol use described as a 'double whammy' for drug and hormone metabolism, beyond alcohol's own direct toxicity?
ch: Alcohol has no interaction with drug metabolism at all

Ethanol above ~100 mg/dL is shunted through the same Zone 3 CYP450 machinery used for ordinary drugs, hormones, and vitamins, so those substrates back up behind the alcohol, get converted to toxic polar metabolites of their own, and pile onto the free-radical injury alcohol is already causing
Alcohol only affects Zone 1 metabolism, leaving Zone 3 drug processing untouched
Alcohol permanently destroys CYP450 enzymes after a single exposure
questions.ex: The 'double whammy' is competition: alcohol's backup oxidation pathway crowds the same Zone 3 CYP450 system that ordinary drugs, hormones, and vitamins rely on, so heavy drinking doesn't just injure the liver directly — it also disrupts normal processing of everything else routed through that same zone, generating additional toxic metabolites on top of alcohol's own free-radical damage.

questions.q: Surgeons plan liver resections around eight functional segments rather than the four anatomic lobes. What is this scheme based on?
ch: External surface landmarks visible on gross inspection alone
The liver's actual internal vascular and biliary branching, independent of its external contour
questions.ex: The eight-segment scheme (segment 1 = the posterior caudate lobe, segments 2-3 = the left lobe's medial and lateral portions, segment 4 = the remaining left-lobe territory, segments 5-8 = the right lobe) is built around internal vascular/biliary branching so surgeons can plan resections that respect the liver's actual internal plumbing, not just its outward shape.

questions.q: Sjögren syndrome can accompany immune-mediated liver disease. What does it cause, and why?
questions.ans: Xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) together, because it targets the salivary and lacrimal glands as a package
questions.note: Worth recognizing as a paired oral/ocular finding rather than just an isolated 'dry mouth' complaint.

questions.q: Primary hemochromatosis typically presents around the fifth decade of life and skews strongly toward men. Why?
ch: It's an autosomal recessive HFE gene defect, and menstrual blood loss offers women a degree of protection by regularly removing iron the disease would otherwise accumulate
Women are genetically immune to HFE mutations
The disease is X-linked and only expressed in males
Presentation timing has no relationship to sex
questions.ex: Primary hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive HFE defect present from birth, but its iron-accumulation effects take decades to become clinically apparent — and in women, regular menstrual blood loss removes iron along the way, delaying (and somewhat blunting) presentation relative to men.

questions.q: How does secondary hemochromatosis differ from primary hemochromatosis?
questions.ans: Secondary hemochromatosis is an acquired iron overload from repeated transfusions or other chronic blood disorders, rather than an inherited HFE mutation
questions.note: Same downstream iron-overload pathology and same special stain, but a different root cause — one genetic, one acquired.

questions.q: How is iron accumulation confirmed histologically in either form of hemochromatosis?
questions.ans: A special iron stain, which shows blue-staining iron granules in hepatocytes
questions.note: Same confirmatory stain regardless of whether the iron overload is primary (genetic) or secondary (transfusion-acquired).

questions.q: A patient with Wilson disease has serum ceruloplasmin measured. What result is actually expected, and why might that seem counterintuitive at first?
ch: Elevated ceruloplasmin, because the liver is trying to compensate by making more of it

LOW ceruloplasmin — it seems counterintuitive because the disease is a copper OVERLOAD state, but the same ATP7B defect that traps copper in the body also disrupts normal ceruloplasmin handling, so the copper-carrier protein itself ends up low
Ceruloplasmin is unaffected by Wilson disease entirely
Ceruloplasmin becomes undetectable, dropping to exactly zero in all cases
questions.ex: This is a genuinely counterintuitive result worth locking in: despite copper accumulating in the liver, brain, and eye, serum ceruloplasmin is LOW, not elevated, because the ATP7B mutation disrupts the machinery that normally loads copper onto ceruloplasmin for secretion — don't let the 'overload disease' framing lead you to guess 'elevated' on a lab-value question.

questions.q: Besides hemangiomas and hepatocellular adenomas, what's another benign liver lesion type worth knowing?
questions.ans: Bile duct hamartomas
questions.note: A benign malformation of bile duct tissue, distinct from the more commonly emphasized vascular (hemangioma) and hepatocellular (adenoma) benign lesions.

questions.q: Imaging shows several discrete lesions scattered through an otherwise normal-looking liver. What should this pattern make you think of first?
ch: A single primary hepatocellular carcinoma that has simply grown in a scattered pattern
Metastatic disease — classically from a colon primary — which is far likelier to produce multiple separate liver lesions than a primary liver tumor is
Hepatic hemangiomas, which always occur in multiples
This pattern is not clinically meaningful
questions.ex: Multiplicity itself is a clue: when imaging shows several discrete liver lesions at once, metastatic disease (classically originating in the colon) is far likelier than a primary liver tumor, which more typically presents as a single dominant mass — a distinct clinical-reasoning point from the separate fact that metastases are also the single most common liver tumor overall.

questions.q: What actually causes the sweet-musty breath odor of fetor hepaticus?
questions.ans: Gut bacteria break down protein into sulfur-containing compounds that are normally absorbed into the portal circulation and cleared by the liver; when liver function fails, those compounds instead reach the systemic circulation and get exhaled by the lungs
questions.note: Same 'liver as a clearance filter' logic as ammonia/urea handling, just with a different gut-bacterial byproduct.

questions.q: Match each finding to the diagnosis it should bring to mind.
pairs: Blue-staining granules on a hepatocyte iron stain
Serum ceruloplasmin that comes back LOW, not high, in a patient with liver disease
Multiple discrete lesions scattered through the liver on imaging
Metastatic disease (classically from a colon primary) rather than a primary liver tumor
Dry eyes and dry mouth together in a patient with immune-mediated liver disease

questions.q: Which of the following best describes vonoprazan's mechanism relative to classic proton pump inhibitors?
ch: It is a reversible potassium-competitive acid blocker that doesn't require actively-secreting pumps
It neutralizes acid directly like an antacid
It is an irreversible PPI with a longer half-life
questions.ex: Vonoprazan is a potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB): unlike the irreversible PPIs, it doesn't need an actively secreting pump to work and can push acid suppression toward 100%. It's newer and costlier, and the lecturer flagged it as background rather than board-tested material.

questions.q: The IBD biologic vedolizumab works by:
ch: Blocking the alpha-4-beta-7 integrin that lets gut-homing T cells cross into the intestinal wall
questions.ex: Vedolizumab blocks gut-specific T-cell trafficking rather than neutralizing a circulating cytokine, which makes it more gut-selective and less systemically immunosuppressive than the anti-TNF biologics — though it sits outside this course's official drug list.

questions.q: Which IBD drug class in this lecture is explicitly NOT considered a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD)?
questions.ex: Glucocorticoids induce remission quickly but aren't disease-modifying in the durable sense the other IBD drug classes are — they're used short-term to control a flare while a true DMARD (aminosalicylate, thiopurine, antifolate, or biologic) takes effect.

questions.q: Activation of which serotonin receptor in the gut drives increased motility rather than nausea?
questions.ex: 5HT3 receptor activation at vagal afferents drives nausea/vomiting (blocked by the 'setron' antiemetics); 5HT4 receptor activation instead stimulates motility — the mechanism behind metoclopramide's prokinetic effect on top of its D2-antagonist antiemetic action.

questions.q: For typical (non-bloody, non-febrile) traveler's diarrhea requiring antibiotics, which two are generally preferred, and when do fluoroquinolones get used instead?
questions.ans: Azithromycin or rifaximin are preferred first; fluoroquinolones are reserved for more severe cases — especially bloody diarrhea with fever — since rifaximin isn't used once fever is present.

questions.q: Beyond recurrent aphthous ulcers, which oral findings can also result from celiac disease's malabsorption, especially if it goes undiagnosed in childhood?
ch: Enamel hypoplasia and delayed tooth eruption
questions.ex: Celiac's malabsorption can affect enamel formation and eruption timing directly — enamel hypoplasia and delayed eruption in a young patient with no other explanation is worth treating as a possible systemic clue, alongside the more commonly cited aphthous ulcers and glossitis.

questions.q: Oral findings of vitamin C deficiency, and its classic (now rare) eponymous disease
questions.ans: Gingival bleeding, delayed healing, and tooth mobility; the classic extreme presentation is scurvy.

questions.q: Why does vitamin K deficiency cause increased oral bleeding?
questions.ans: Vitamin K is required for the coagulation cascade (synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X), so deficiency impairs clotting and raises bleeding risk, including gingival bleeding.

questions.q: Primary oral finding of protein deficiency
questions.ans: Delayed wound healing

questions.q: A patient reports right upper quadrant pain that radiates to the right shoulder after a fatty meal. This is most consistent with:
questions.ex: Gallbladder disease (biliary colic/cholecystitis) classically presents with right upper quadrant pain that can refer to the right shoulder, often triggered by a fatty meal that stimulates gallbladder contraction against an obstructed or inflamed system.

questions.q: What is the main dental-chair significance of a patient having a history of pancreatitis?
ch: It has no bearing on dental treatment
It's a prompt to screen for alcohol use and avoid acetaminophen if the patient drinks heavily, since the liver may already be stressed
It requires antibiotic prophylaxis before any dental procedure
It means local anesthetic is contraindicated
questions.ex: Pancreatitis is strongly tied to alcohol abuse; a patient with this history may also have compromised liver reserve, making acetaminophen (processed by the liver) a medication to use cautiously or avoid — the same reasoning applied to any patient with a heavy-drinking history.

questions.q: A patient on long-term oral corticosteroids needs a surgical extraction. What is the physiologic concern, and how is it typically managed?
ch: Increased infection risk only; manage with antibiotics alone
Suppressed adrenal cortisol production means the body can't mount its normal stress response to the procedure; a physician-coordinated supplemental ('stress') dose may be needed
Corticosteroids have no relevant interaction with dental surgery
questions.ex: Exogenous corticosteroids suppress the adrenal glands' own cortisol production. A procedure that would normally trigger a stress-hormone surge — like an extraction — may need to be covered with a supplemental corticosteroid dose, coordinated with the patient's physician, on top of expecting delayed healing.

questions.q: Which INR value should prompt deferring ALL surgical dental treatment, including periodontal probing, until cleared with the patient's physician?
questions.ex: Normal INR is about 1.0; a therapeutically anticoagulated patient is often managed around 2.5; an INR of 3.5 or higher is high enough bleeding risk that even routine periodontal probing should wait until it's addressed medically.

questions.q: Why does a dry mouth undermine denture retention even when the denture itself fits well?
questions.ans: Denture retention depends partly on a thin film of saliva forming a suction-like seal between the denture and the mucosa — without adequate saliva, that seal is lost regardless of how well the denture is shaped, the same way a glass loses its 'stick' to a polished table once the condensation dries.

questions.q: Why are patients on several medications especially likely to have dry mouth?
questions.ans: The large majority of medications reduce salivary flow as a side effect — only a small number of drugs are specifically designed to increase it — so polypharmacy compounds xerostomia risk.

questions.q: After a fatty meal, an enterocyte re-esterifies absorbed monoglycerides and fatty acids into triglycerides and packages them into chylomicrons for exit at the basolateral membrane. Which structure in the villus core receives these chylomicrons, as opposed to the glycerol and short/medium-chain fatty acids that enter the blood capillaries directly?
ch: The blood capillary network within the villus
The central lacteal (the villus's lymphatic capillary)
questions.ex: Chylomicrons are too large to readily enter blood capillaries and instead pass into the more permeable central lacteal in the villus core; smaller, more water-soluble absorption products like glycerol and short/medium-chain fatty acids diffuse directly into the blood capillaries instead.

questions.q: Secretory IgA found in small-intestinal luminal secretions is produced by which cell type, and in what form?
ch: Plasma cells in the lamina propria, as a dimer
questions.ex: Plasma cells in the lamina propria synthesize IgA as a dimer, which is then transported across the overlying epithelial cell and released into the lumen -- the same dimeric, plasma-cell-derived form of IgA seen in saliva.

questions.q: Which of these is a distinctive gross feature unique to the large intestine, formed by three longitudinal bands of thickened muscularis externa whose tonic contraction puckers the bowel wall into pouch-like sacculations?
questions.ex: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal smooth-muscle bands running the length of the colon; because they are shorter than the bowel wall, their tonic contraction puckers the colon into the haustra -- a feature absent from the small intestine, which instead has plicae and villi.

questions.q: Hepatocytes in zone 1 (adjacent to the portal triad) receive the most highly oxygenated blood; those in zone 3 (adjacent to the central vein) receive the least, since oxygen is extracted as blood flows from the portal triad toward the central vein. If hepatic arterial flow is acutely compromised, which zone suffers first, and which zone is normally the most metabolically active?
ch: Zone 1 is compromised first; zone 3 is most metabolically active
Zone 3 is compromised first; zone 1 is most metabolically active
Zone 2 is compromised first; zone 1 is most metabolically active
Zone 1 and zone 3 are equally vulnerable; zone 2 is most metabolically active
questions.ex: Because blood flows from the portal triad (zone 1) toward the central vein (zone 3), oxygen is progressively depleted, making zone 3 the most hypoxia-vulnerable region when arterial supply drops; zone 1, bathed in the freshest oxygenated blood, sustains the liver's most energy-demanding functions.

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of total hepatic blood flow arrives via the portal vein versus the proper hepatic artery, and how does oxygenation differ between the two?
ch: About 80% via the hepatic artery (oxygenated); about 20% via the portal vein (mostly deoxygenated)
About 50% via each vessel, both carrying oxygenated blood
About 80% via the portal vein (mostly deoxygenated); about 20% via the hepatic artery (oxygenated)
About 80% via the portal vein (oxygenated); about 20% via the hepatic artery (deoxygenated)
questions.ex: The portal vein contributes the large majority of hepatic blood flow -- nutrient-rich but deoxygenated blood draining the GI tract -- while the smaller-caliber proper hepatic artery, a celiac trunk branch, supplies the minority volume but delivers oxygenated blood.

questions.q: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells normally store vitamin A within the Space of Disse. What happens to these cells in chronic liver injury?
ch: They become activated and produce the collagen deposition seen in liver fibrosis
They differentiate into Kupffer cells and increase phagocytic activity
They proliferate to directly regenerate hepatocytes
They migrate into the bile canaliculi and obstruct bile flow
questions.ex: With chronic injury, the normally quiescent, vitamin-A-storing stellate cells activate into myofibroblast-like, collagen-producing cells -- the same cell responsible for vitamin A storage becomes the source of the fibrosis seen in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis when repeatedly injured.

questions.q: Of the bile salts that enter the duodenum, approximately what fraction is reabsorbed in the intestine and recirculated back to the liver, versus newly synthesized by hepatocytes?
ch: Essentially all bile salts are newly synthesized each cycle; none are recirculated
questions.ex: Bile salts undergo efficient enterohepatic circulation -- the large majority are reabsorbed in the intestine and returned to the liver via the portal vein for re-secretion, so hepatocytes need to synthesize only a small fraction fresh to maintain the bile salt pool.

questions.q: A patient reports bloating, gas, and osmotic diarrhea after drinking milk, but tolerates table sugar (sucrose) and starchy foods without symptoms. A deficiency of which brush-border enzyme best explains this pattern?
questions.ex: Lactase is the brush-border enzyme that cleaves lactose (the disaccharide in milk) into glucose and galactose; without it, undigested lactose stays in the lumen, draws water osmotically, and is fermented by colonic bacteria, causing gas and diarrhea. Sucrase and maltase/isomaltase are separate, substrate-specific enzymes, so sucrose and starch digestion are unaffected.

questions.q: Carbohydrate digestion is often used as the classic example of "luminal" and "contact" digestion working together. Which pairing correctly matches each enzyme type to where it acts?
ch: Salivary/pancreatic amylase acts in the lumen; brush-border disaccharidases act at the enterocyte surface
Salivary/pancreatic amylase acts at the enterocyte surface; brush-border disaccharidases act in the lumen
Both amylase and the disaccharidases act freely in the luminal contents
Both amylase and the disaccharidases are bound to the brush border
questions.ex: Amylase is secreted into the gut lumen (saliva, pancreatic juice) and digests starch there -- luminal digestion. The disaccharidases (lactase, sucrase, maltase/isomaltase) are anchored to the brush border, so sugars must contact the enterocyte surface to be digested -- contact digestion.

questions.q: Fructose has its own dedicated apical transporter, distinct from the one used by glucose and galactose. What is this transporter, and how does it move fructose into the enterocyte?
ch: SGLT1; secondary active transport co-transported with Na+
GLUT5; facilitated diffusion down its own concentration gradient
GLUT2; primary active transport requiring ATP
questions.ex: Fructose crosses the apical membrane via GLUT5, which -- unlike SGLT1 -- is not sodium-coupled; it works by simple facilitated diffusion, so it only moves fructose in when luminal concentration exceeds intracellular concentration. All three monosaccharides then exit together into the blood via GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane.

questions.q: Compared to absorbing three free amino acids individually via their sodium-dependent transporters, absorbing the nutritional equivalent as a single tripeptide via PEPT1 is:
ch: Slower, because PEPT1 has a much lower turnover rate than amino acid transporters
Kinetically more efficient, because one PEPT1 turnover delivers multiple amino acids at once
Equally fast, since both are secondary active transport using the same sodium gradient
Impossible, because tripeptides cannot cross the apical membrane intact
questions.ex: Each PEPT1 turnover carries an entire di-/tripeptide (2-3 amino acids) in one step, versus one amino acid per turnover of a single amino acid transporter -- this efficiency was demonstrated by showing glycine appears in the blood faster when fed as the dipeptide glycylglycine than as free glycine.

questions.q: A patient with cystic fibrosis has a defective CFTR channel in pancreatic duct cells. Which of the following best explains the resulting pancreatic insufficiency and increased risk of pancreatitis?
ch: Acinar cells stop producing digestive enzymes entirely

Without functional CFTR, insufficient chloride (and bicarbonate) is secreted into the duct lumen, so enzyme-rich secretions cannot be washed out of the ducts, and enzymes accumulate and activate within the pancreas
CCK receptors on the acinar cell are downregulated, halting enzyme release
The sphincter of Oddi remains permanently contracted, blocking the ampulla of Vater
questions.ex: CFTR is the apical chloride (and bicarbonate) channel on pancreatic duct cells, driving the bulk of pancreatic fluid secretion. Without it, ductal secretion fails, protein-rich acinar output can't be flushed out, ducts become obstructed, and enzymes are retained and autoactivate -- causing pancreatitis, and, since enzymes never reach the gut, malabsorption.

questions.q: A patient with a gallstone obstructing the common bile duct develops jaundice. Which pattern of bilirubin elevation would you expect, and why?
ch: Elevated unconjugated bilirubin, because red blood cell breakdown has increased
Elevated unconjugated bilirubin, because the liver cannot conjugate bilirubin to glucuronic acid
Elevated conjugated bilirubin, because bile already conjugated by the liver cannot exit into the duodenum and backs up into the blood
No change in bilirubin, since obstruction only affects bile acids, not bilirubin
questions.ex: This is post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice -- bilirubin was already conjugated normally by the liver, but the physical blockage prevents it draining into the duodenum, so it backs up into the blood as conjugated bilirubin. Contrast with prehepatic jaundice (hemolysis overwhelms conjugation, elevating unconjugated bilirubin) and intrahepatic jaundice (impaired conjugation itself, e.g. cirrhosis or hepatitis).

questions.q: Deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid are classified as "secondary" bile acids rather than "primary" bile acids. What accounts for this distinction?
ch: They are synthesized directly by hepatocytes from cholesterol, unlike primary bile acids
They are produced when gut bacteria remove the 7-alpha-hydroxyl group from primary bile acids via dehydroxylation
They are conjugated to taurine while primary bile acids are conjugated to glycine
They are sulfated derivatives that make up the majority of the total bile acid pool
questions.ex: Primary bile acids (cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid) are made directly by the liver from cholesterol. Gut bacteria then dehydroxylate them, removing the 7-alpha-OH group, yielding secondary bile acids (deoxycholic, lithocholic acid). Conjugation to glycine/taurine is a separate, liver-driven solubility modification, independent of the primary/secondary distinction.

questions.q: Pancreatic ductal secretion remains isotonic across all flow rates, even though its chloride and bicarbonate concentrations vary reciprocally with flow. How does this compare to salivary gland secretion?
ch: Salivary secretion is also isotonic at all flow rates, just like pancreatic secretion
Salivary secretion becomes hypotonic relative to plasma, especially at low flow rates, unlike pancreatic secretion
Salivary secretion is always hypertonic to plasma, while pancreatic secretion is always hypotonic
Neither gland's secretion tonicity is physiologically relevant
questions.ex: The pancreatic duct's transport mechanisms keep its secretion isotonic to plasma at every flow rate -- only the Cl-/HCO3- ratio shifts (chloride-dominant at low flow, bicarbonate-dominant at high flow). This is explicitly different from the salivary duct, which reabsorbs more solute than water and renders saliva hypotonic.

questions.q: The liver's sinusoids contain resident macrophages that intercept blood arriving directly from the gut. What is the name of these cells, and what is their primary protective role?
ch: Kupffer cells -- resident sinusoidal macrophages that phagocytose bacteria arriving in portal blood, preventing systemic bacteremia
Hepatic stellate cells -- vitamin A-storing pericytes that become phagocytic once activated
Cholangiocytes -- biliary epithelial cells that filter bacteria out of portal blood before bile secretion
Portal fibroblasts -- connective tissue cells that wall off infected portal tracts with collagen
questions.ex: Kupffer cells sit within the sinusoidal lumen, the first liver structure portal blood contacts. Since essentially all gut-derived blood passes through the liver before reaching systemic circulation, Kupffer cells act as a first line of defense, phagocytosing bacteria that escape the gut and preventing systemic infection.

questions.q: A patient in hypovolemic shock develops transiently elevated liver enzymes from hepatic hypoperfusion. Which zone of the liver lobule is injured first, and why?
ch: Zone 3 (pericentral) -- it is farthest from the incoming portal/arterial blood and already has the lowest baseline oxygen tension
Zone 1 (periportal) -- it receives the highest concentration of circulating toxins and is the most metabolically active zone
Zone 2 -- it sits at a watershed between the two blood supplies and receives no direct perfusion from either vessel
Zone 1 (periportal) -- it extracts the most oxygen first, leaving none for the deeper zones
questions.ex: Oxygen delivery falls off along the sinusoid from Zone 1 (richest, first to receive portal venous and hepatic arterial blood) to Zone 3 (poorest, farthest from the incoming supply). During any state of reduced perfusion, Zone 3 hepatocytes are already running on the least oxygen reserve, so they become hypoxic and necrose first -- the classic mechanism behind centrilobular/shock liver injury, distinct from Zone 3's separate vulnerability to acetaminophen via CYP450 enzyme concentration.

questions.q: On liver biopsy from a patient with acute viral hepatitis, the pathologist identifies small, round, intensely eosinophilic structures within the lobules, each representing a single dying hepatocyte extruded from the liver cell plate. What are these called, and what process do they represent?
ch: Acidophil bodies (Councilman bodies) -- individual hepatocytes undergoing apoptosis
Mallory-Denk bodies -- hepatocytes undergoing fatty degeneration
Ground-glass hepatocytes -- hepatocytes packed with viral surface antigen
Bile infarcts -- hepatocytes destroyed by extravasated bile
questions.ex: Acidophil (Councilman) bodies are shrunken, intensely eosinophilic remnants of single apoptotic hepatocytes -- a classic finding in acute viral hepatitis reflecting immune-mediated killing of individual infected cells, as opposed to confluent necrosis. Mallory-Denk bodies are a different eosinophilic inclusion associated with alcoholic/fatty liver disease, not apoptosis.

questions.q: A liver biopsy from a patient with a long history of heavy alcohol use shows ballooning hepatocyte degeneration and eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions composed of damaged intermediate filaments. What are these inclusions called, and with which condition are they classically associated?
questions.ex: Mallory-Denk bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of damaged, aggregated intermediate filaments seen in ballooned hepatocytes -- classically in alcoholic steatohepatitis (also seen in NASH). They represent a degenerative change distinct from apoptosis (acidophil/Councilman bodies).

questions.q: A dental patient with longstanding cholestatic liver disease presents with cheilitis (lip inflammation) and a smooth, atrophic tongue. What is the most likely mechanism linking these oral findings to the patient's liver disease?
ch: Impaired bile secretion causes malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins and other nutrients, producing deficiencies that manifest in the oral mucosa
Elevated unconjugated bilirubin directly stains and irritates the oral mucosa
Reduced hepatic clotting factor synthesis causes microhemorrhages in the lip and tongue mucosa
Ammonia accumulation from impaired hepatic detoxification directly damages the oral epithelium
questions.ex: Bile is required for absorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins; when hepatic excretory/bile function is impaired, the resulting malabsorption produces nutritional and vitamin deficiencies that classically show up in the oral cavity as cheilitis, a smooth/atrophic tongue, and perioral rash -- distinct from the jaundice and bleeding tendency also seen in liver disease.

questions.q: Which of the following gastric/GI tumors arises from the neuroendocrine cells of the mucosa (in the stomach, often the gastrin-producing cells), occurs most commonly in the stomach and small intestine, and was historically referred to as a "carcinoid tumor"?
questions.ex: Neuroendocrine tumors arise from the diffuse neuroendocrine cell population of the GI mucosa -- gastrin-producing cells in the stomach -- and are most common in the stomach and small intestine. "Carcinoid tumor" is the older term for these, distinguishing them from GIST (mesenchymal, submucosal, CKIT-driven) and MALT lymphoma (B-cell, H. pylori-associated).

questions.q: A middle-aged patient has chronic watery diarrhea with a grossly and endoscopically normal-appearing colon. Biopsy reveals a markedly thickened band of collagen immediately beneath the surface epithelium. This is diagnostic of which subtype of microscopic colitis?
questions.ex: Microscopic colitis has two histologic subtypes that both present identically (normal-looking colon on colonoscopy, watery diarrhea): lymphocytic colitis, defined by increased intraepithelial lymphocytes without a thickened collagen band, and collagenous colitis, defined by a markedly thickened subepithelial collagen band.

questions.q: Before starting a patient with Crohn's disease on azathioprine, testing for a polymorphism in which enzyme is recommended to predict the risk of severe drug toxicity from slowed drug metabolism?
questions.ex: Azathioprine is a prodrug partly metabolized by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT). Patients with a slow-metabolizer TPMT polymorphism clear the active thioguanine nucleotides more slowly, so drug levels build up and severe bone marrow suppression/toxicity can follow -- which is why genotyping before starting azathioprine is recommended. Flagged in lecture as a likely board topic.

questions.q: A patient has been taking large amounts of calcium carbonate antacid tablets daily for months and presents with hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and acute kidney injury. This classic triad from excessive calcium plus alkali intake is known as:
questions.ex: Milk-alkali syndrome results from excessive intake of an absorbable calcium source (calcium carbonate antacids, calcium-containing dairy) together with alkali, producing hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renal insufficiency -- historically common when calcium-containing antacids were a mainstay of ulcer treatment, but still seen with heavy antacid/calcium-supplement use today.

questions.q: A patient is given a transdermal muscarinic-receptor-antagonist patch that blocks the neural pathway from the vestibular apparatus to the brainstem, to be applied before a cruise. Which statement correctly describes appropriate use of this drug (scopolamine)?
ch: It works primarily by blocking D2 receptors in the area postrema
It is equally effective whether given before or after symptoms begin
It is a first-generation antihistamine rather than an anticholinergic
It is far more effective when given before symptom onset than after symptoms have started
questions.ex: Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist that blocks the inner-ear-to-brainstem pathway responsible for motion sickness; it is used preventatively (patch before travel, or before surgery for PONV prophylaxis) and is much less effective once nausea has already started. As a classic anticholinergic, its adverse effects include xerostomia, blurred vision, and mydriasis -- directly relevant chairside since dry mouth is easy to spot on a dental exam.

questions.q: A patient taking large amounts of bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) for traveler's diarrhea presents to the dental office worried about GI bleeding after noticing black discoloration of her tongue and stool. What is the correct explanation?
ch: This represents oral candidiasis and needs antifungal treatment
This indicates active upper GI hemorrhage and requires immediate referral
This is a hypersensitivity reaction to the salicylate component and the drug should be stopped immediately
Bismuth combines with hydrogen sulfide in the gut to form bismuth sulfide, a harmless black pigment -- not blood
questions.ex: Bismuth subsalicylate reacts with trace hydrogen sulfide in the GI tract to form bismuth sulfide, a black, entirely harmless precipitate that darkens the tongue and stool. This commonly alarms patients (and can alarm a dentist examining the tongue) but does not indicate GI bleeding.

questions.q: Just before a patient vomits, their mouth typically becomes noticeably wet with saliva. What is the physiological purpose of this pre-emetic hypersalivation?
ch: It dilutes stomach acid before it is expelled, reducing systemic absorption of toxins
It creates a protective barrier that helps shield the teeth from the acidic gastric contents about to be expelled
It lubricates the esophagus to prevent mechanical injury during forceful expulsion of stomach contents
It signals the chemoreceptor trigger zone to end the vomiting reflex once enough saliva has been produced
questions.ex: Vomitus is highly acidic, and repeated acid exposure erodes enamel; the reflexive hypersalivation right before vomiting coats the teeth with saliva as a protective buffer before that acid arrives -- the same buffering logic behind why patients shouldn't brush immediately after an acid exposure.

questions.q: During the vomiting reflex, the glottis normally closes as the soft palate rises to protect the airway. In which clinical setting is loss of this protective reflex a well-recognized cause of a serious pulmonary complication, and what is that complication?
