ch: Patients with GERD, who can develop chronic bronchitis
Heavily sedated patients, who can develop aspiration pneumonia
Patients with cystic fibrosis, who can develop a pneumothorax
Pregnant patients, who can develop pulmonary edema
questions.ex: Sedation blunts protective airway reflexes, so if a sedated patient vomits, the glottis may fail to close in time and gastric contents can be aspirated into the lungs -- a key patient-safety concern whenever dental sedation or general anesthesia is used.

questions.q: Ondansetron (Zofran) controls nausea/vomiting triggered by surgery or chemotherapy primarily by acting at which site, distinct from the site targeted by antihistamines and anticholinergics?
ch: The vestibular apparatus of the inner ear
questions.ex: Antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine) and anticholinergics (e.g., scopolamine) act at the chemoreceptor trigger zone, while 5-HT3-targeting drugs like ondansetron act at the nucleus tractus solitarius -- the same region triggered by surgery/chemo -- which is why matching the agent to the pathway driving a given patient's nausea (or combining agents) matters.

questions.q: A 58-year-old patient reports several months of epigastric pain and has been taking ibuprofen daily for chronic joint pain. Recent bloodwork shows mild anemia. Which underlying process best explains this presentation?
ch: Gastroesophageal reflux disease caused by chronic NSAID use, with anemia from malabsorption
Peptic ulcer disease caused by chronic NSAID use, with anemia from chronic GI blood loss
Crohn's disease caused by chronic NSAID use, with anemia from vitamin B12 malabsorption
Acute pancreatitis caused by chronic NSAID use, with anemia from bone marrow suppression
questions.ex: Chronic NSAID use (ibuprofen, naproxen) is a classic cause of peptic ulcer disease independent of H. pylori, and a bleeding ulcer causes slow chronic GI blood loss presenting as iron-deficiency anemia -- directly relevant to dental practice since dentists routinely recommend/prescribe NSAIDs for pain control.

questions.q: A patient with burning mouth syndrome needs short-term symptomatic relief. The lecture describes a compounded "magic mouthwash" for this. Which combination of ingredients (and purposes) matches what was described?
ch: Chlorhexidine for antisepsis, hydrocortisone for inflammation, and sodium bicarbonate to neutralize oral pH
Nystatin for antifungal coverage, viscous lidocaine for numbing, and hydrogen peroxide for debridement
Viscous lidocaine for numbing, diphenhydramine for its anti-inflammatory/antihistamine effect, and an antacid (e.g., Maalox) for viscosity so the mixture coats the tissue longer
Benzocaine for numbing, triamcinolone for inflammation, and artificial saliva for lubrication
questions.ex: Magic mouthwash is described as a short-term compounded rinse combining viscous lidocaine for topical numbing, diphenhydramine for its anti-inflammatory/antihistamine effect, and an antacid like Maalox mainly to thicken the mixture so it clings to the mucosa long enough for the other ingredients to work.

questions.q: Two patients present with dental erosion. Patient 1's erosion is concentrated on the lingual/palatal surfaces of the maxillary teeth with visible translucency near the DEJ. Patient 2 has more generalized erosion across most tooth surfaces. Based on the exposure-pattern logic taught in lecture, what does this difference suggest?
ch: Patient 1's pattern suggests extrinsic dietary acid, while Patient 2's pattern suggests GERD
Both patterns are equally consistent with GERD; distribution doesn't help distinguish etiology
Patient 1's pattern suggests an intrinsic source (e.g., GERD), while Patient 2's pattern suggests extrinsic/dietary acid exposure
Patient 1's pattern is diagnostic of Sjogren's syndrome rather than an acid-related process
questions.ex: Acid refluxing up from the stomach in GERD reaches the mouth from behind the tongue, so it exposes the lingual/palatal surfaces first and most severely; acid taken in through the mouth (diet) contacts all tooth surfaces more evenly -- exactly why lingual/palatal erosion is the classic sign of GERD specifically.

questions.q: According to the lecture's board-review pearls, why is it clinically significant that a dentist may be the first provider to notice signs of Crohn's disease?
ch: Because Crohn's disease exclusively affects the oral cavity and never involves the intestines
Because oral lesions (aphthous-like ulcers, cobblestone mucosa, lip swelling/granulomatosis) can appear before intestinal symptoms of Crohn's disease develop
Because dental radiographs are the gold-standard diagnostic test for Crohn's disease
Because periodontal probing depths are pathognomonic for Crohn's disease
questions.ex: The lecture explicitly flags that Crohn's oral manifestations can precede GI symptoms, so a dentist who recognizes cobblestone mucosa, granulomatous lip swelling, or recurrent aphthous-type ulcers may trigger the earliest referral for a diagnosis the patient doesn't know they need yet -- a distinct, diagnostic-timing point from simply knowing which oral findings occur in Crohn's.

questions.q: A 54-year-old with known cirrhosis and esophageal varices (dilated, thin-walled submucosal veins from chronic portal hypertension) presents with hematemesis. Octreotide is started emergently as a bridge to endoscopy. What is the pharmacologic basis for using this drug in acute variceal hemorrhage?
ch: It replenishes the clotting factors the liver can no longer synthesize, correcting the coagulopathy driving the bleed
As a somatostatin analog, it constricts splanchnic blood flow, lowering pressure in the portal system (and the varices it feeds)
It directly seals the ruptured vein via a local vasoconstrictive effect at the bleeding site, similar to an endoscopic clip
It blocks the H+/K+-ATPase, raising gastric pH to protect the bleeding varix from acid exposure
questions.ex: Octreotide is a synthetic somatostatin analog that, among its other effects, reduces splanchnic blood flow; lowering portal venous inflow lowers pressure in the varices themselves, which is why it's used as a bridge to endoscopic therapy in acute variceal hemorrhage. It has no direct effect on hepatic clotting-factor synthesis and no PPI-like effect on gastric acid.

questions.q: A patient has episodic facial flushing, watery diarrhea, and wheezing. Workup finds a small-bowel mass and a new murmur consistent with tricuspid regurgitation; biopsy of the mass shows a neuroendocrine tumor. Which of the following best explains this patient's systemic symptoms, and which drug directly targets the underlying hormonal excess?
ch: Excess gastrin release; treat with a proton pump inhibitor
Excess serotonin (and other vasoactive substances) released by the tumor; treat with octreotide
Excess VIP release; treat with loperamide
Ectopic ACTH release; treat with ketoconazole
questions.ex: This is carcinoid syndrome: a neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor -- the same tumor type covered as arising from the GI mucosa's neuroendocrine cells -- secretes serotonin and other vasoactive substances, producing flushing, secretory diarrhea, bronchospasm, and, over time, right-sided valvular fibrosis. Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, is used to control the hormonal symptoms of carcinoid syndrome, distinguishing this from a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison, treated with a PPI) or a VIPoma (treated with octreotide as well, but driven by VIP rather than serotonin).

questions.q: A gallstone becomes impacted at the ampulla of Vater, obstructing both the distal common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. Which combination of findings would this dual obstruction be expected to produce?
ch: Elevated unconjugated bilirubin (from impaired hepatic conjugation) plus low serum lipase, since pancreatic outflow is blocked

Elevated conjugated bilirubin (bile already conjugated by the liver cannot drain into the duodenum) plus elevated serum lipase/amylase, as trapped pancreatic secretions let trypsinogen autoactivate to trypsin, which activates the rest of the zymogen cascade and causes autodigestion
Normal bilirubin, since only the pancreatic duct is meaningfully obstructed, plus elevated unconjugated bilirubin from a coexisting hemolytic process
Elevated conjugated bilirubin only; acinar cells keep secreting normally regardless of ductal patency, so pancreatic enzymes are unaffected
questions.ex: A stone at the ampulla backs up both systems at once. Bile the liver already conjugated can't drain -- the same obstructive-jaundice logic as any distal biliary obstruction, producing a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Meanwhile, trapped pancreatic secretions let trypsinogen autoactivate to trypsin, which in turn activates chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and the procarboxypeptidases -- the same cascade that makes enteropeptidase deficiency cripple digestion of essentially all dietary protein -- except here it runs unchecked inside the pancreas itself, causing autodigestion (pancreatitis, with its lipase/amylase elevation).

questions.q: A 19-year-old with cystic fibrosis, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and bulky, greasy stools is scheduled for a surgical extraction. He admits he hasn't been taking his prescribed pancreatic enzyme replacement consistently. Which additional consideration is most important before proceeding, and why?
ch: Checking a coagulation panel (e.g., PT/INR), because chronic pancreatic enzyme insufficiency impairs fat digestion, and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamin K can impair synthesis of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
No additional workup is needed; cystic fibrosis has no bearing on bleeding risk
Checking serum calcium, because pancreatic insufficiency directly causes hypocalcemia-driven bleeding
Prescribing prophylactic antibiotics, since cystic fibrosis is itself a standard indication for antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures
questions.ex: Without adequate pancreatic lipase, fat digestion fails and the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) -- absorbed alongside dietary fat in mixed micelles -- go unabsorbed with it. Vitamin K is required to synthesize clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, so a patient with poorly controlled exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (from defective CFTR-driven ductal secretion, as in cystic fibrosis) can develop a real bleeding risk before any procedure, independent of platelet count -- worth a coagulation panel before a surgical extraction.

questions.q: A patient with a 15-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with tender hepatomegaly. Labs show AST 220 U/L and ALT 90 U/L. Liver biopsy shows hepatocyte ballooning with eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions. Which stage of alcoholic liver disease does this represent, and what accounts for the specific AST:ALT pattern?
ch: Simple steatosis; the AST:ALT ratio is not meaningful at this stage

Alcoholic steatohepatitis (the ballooning-plus-Mallory-Denk-bodies stage); AST:ALT > 2 reflects mitochondrial injury, since AST is partly mitochondrial and needs more severe injury to be released, while ALT (purely cytosolic) leaks with even mild injury
Cirrhosis; the AST:ALT ratio here mainly reflects loss of total hepatocyte mass rather than the type of injury
Autoimmune hepatitis superimposed on fatty liver; the AST:ALT ratio tracks autoantibody titers
questions.ex: Ballooning degeneration plus Mallory-Denk bodies (damaged, aggregated intermediate filaments) marks the steatohepatitis stage of alcoholic liver disease -- past reversible steatosis but short of irreversible fibrosis/cirrhosis. An AST:ALT ratio above 2:1 is a classic clue specifically because ALT sits in the cytosol and leaks out with even mild hepatocyte injury, while AST is partly mitochondrial and only releases in quantity once injury is severe enough to damage mitochondria -- exactly what sustained heavy alcohol exposure does.

questions.q: Two patients need antiemetic therapy for different triggers. Patient 1 is about to start cisplatin chemotherapy, a potent activator of the chemoreceptor trigger zone via serotonin release. Patient 2 has severe motion sickness on a cruise, driven by the vestibular apparatus. Which drug-to-mechanism pairing best matches each patient's trigger?
ch: Patient 1: ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist acting on the serotonin pathway the CTZ and gut rely on; Patient 2: scopolamine, a muscarinic antagonist blocking the vestibular-to-brainstem pathway
Patient 1: scopolamine; Patient 2: ondansetron -- the two mechanisms are interchangeable regardless of the trigger
Both patients should receive the same first-generation antihistamine, since every nausea trigger converges equally on histamine receptors
questions.ex: The area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone) integrates serotonin (5-HT3), substance P (NK1), dopamine (D2), muscarinic, cannabinoid, and opioid signals. Chemotherapy classically triggers it via serotonin released from damaged enterochromaffin cells, which is why a 5-HT3 antagonist like ondansetron -- acting downstream at the nucleus tractus solitarius -- is first-line. Motion sickness instead arises from the vestibular apparatus signaling through a muscarinic pathway, which is why scopolamine -- a muscarinic antagonist that only works well when given before symptoms start -- is preferred there instead. Matching the antiemetic class to the actual trigger pathway, rather than using any antiemetic interchangeably, is the key lesson.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents to a dental clinic with painful aphthous-like ulcers, cobblestone-appearing buccal mucosa, and granulomatous lip swelling, but denies any GI symptoms. The dentist refers him for a GI workup, which reveals transmural inflammation with skip lesions and a perianal fistula, confirming Crohn's disease. Before starting azathioprine, which additional step is indicated, and why?
ch: None; azathioprine can be started immediately at a standard dose
Testing thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity, since slow metabolizers are at risk of severe bone marrow suppression from azathioprine
A CYP2D6 genotype test, since azathioprine is primarily metabolized by that enzyme
A baseline INR, since azathioprine's main risk is bleeding
questions.ex: This patient's oral findings -- aphthous-type ulcers, cobblestone mucosa, granulomatous lip swelling -- are classic for Crohn's disease and, as this course's own dental lecture emphasizes, can appear before intestinal symptoms develop, making a dentist a possible first point of diagnosis. The perianal fistula reflects Crohn's transmural, full-bowel-wall-thickness inflammation, which -- unlike ulcerative colitis's mucosa-limited disease -- lets chronic inflammation tunnel into adjacent structures. Before starting azathioprine for this diagnosis, TPMT testing is recommended: a slow-metabolizer polymorphism clears the active thioguanine nucleotides more slowly, risking severe toxicity/bone marrow suppression at a standard dose.
